paragraphs: The bridge's central span, at 1,991 metres, held the record for the longest of any suspension bridge for nearly a quarter century, an unusually long reign in a field where records typically fall within a decade or two. Its towers were designed to survive the kind of earthquake that struck nearby Kobe in January 1995, during construction, which shifted the towers apart by roughly a metre and forced engineers to lengthen the span to match.

Turkey's 1915 Canakkale Bridge overtook it in March 2022 by only 32 metres, ending the Akashi Kaikyo's run at just under twenty-four years. It still carries Japan's Kobe-Naruto expressway across the Akashi Strait, a stretch of water notorious for strong tidal currents that made the crossing dangerous for ferries before the bridge existed.

Baltic amber turns up in graves nowhere near the Baltic. Egyptian tombs and Mycenaean burial sites from the second millennium BCE have yielded beads of it, fossilised tree resin gathered on beaches in what is now Poland and Lithuania and carried south over land and river for many hundreds of kilometres.

No single caravan made that whole journey. Amber most likely passed through a chain of local traders, river by river down toward the Danube and the Adriatic, exchanged along the way for salt, metal or textiles. The route later took a name, the Amber Road, but in the Bronze Age it was a relay rather than a road.

Ancestral Puebloan builders fitted their cliff dwellings into natural alcoves worn into canyon walls by wind and water, rather than carving the rock themselves. The overhang above did the work a roof would otherwise need to do, keeping stone and mortar structures dry for centuries and shading them from the harsh summer sun of the Southwest.

Sites such as Mesa Verde grew crowded through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries as communities that had farmed the mesa tops above moved down into these sheltered ledges. Reaching some dwellings required climbing hand and toeholds cut directly into the rock face, a layout that also made the settlements easier to defend.

Angkor's temples are the part visitors see, but the Khmer Empire's real achievement underneath them was water. Vast reservoirs called barays and an extensive network of canals stored monsoon rainfall and released it through the dry season, letting Angkor support farmland and a population far larger than the surrounding terrain could otherwise feed.

That system reached its fullest extent around the mid twelfth century, the period that also produced Angkor Wat under Suryavarman II. Some historians now argue the hydraulic network's later strain, silting canals and shifting rainfall, contributed as much to Angkor's eventual decline as any of the military pressures it faced from neighbouring kingdoms.

Most Anglo-Saxon buildings were timber, which is why the stone churches at Monkwearmouth and Jarrow, founded in 674 and 682 by the nobleman Benedict Biscop, stand out: he brought masons from Gaul because England had largely lost the skill of building in dressed stone since the Romans left.

Jarrow's monastery raised the monk Bede, whose historical writing survives partly because the community around him kept a working scriptorium. The dedication stone at Jarrow, dated 685, is one of the few Anglo-Saxon building inscriptions to survive in its original place.

Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and Ronald Wayne formed Apple Computer on 1 April 1976 in Jobs's family garage in Los Altos, California, to sell a circuit board Wozniak had built, the Apple I. Wayne sold his 10 percent stake back to the other two for 800 dollars within two weeks, a decision that would have been worth billions had he kept it.

Wozniak designed the machine largely for his own enjoyment at the Homebrew Computer Club, a hobbyist group where members traded schematics rather than money. Jobs's contribution was recognising it could be sold rather than just built, and the pair financed the first batch of about 200 units by Jobs selling his Volkswagen van and Wozniak selling a programmable calculator.

Apple Park opened to staff in April 2017 on a Cupertino site that had previously been Hewlett-Packard's campus. Steve Jobs presented the design to the city council himself in 2011, less than a year before his death, describing a ring-shaped building large enough to hold roughly twelve thousand employees.

The ring is almost a kilometre around, clad entirely in curved glass, and sits inside grounds planted with over nine thousand drought-tolerant trees chosen to resemble the orchards that once covered the Santa Clara Valley before it became known for anything else.

The Pont du Gard carries a channel of water, not a road, across the Gardon river valley in southern France. It was one link in a roughly 50 kilometre aqueduct feeding the Roman colony of Nemausus, modern Nimes, and its three tiers of arches drop only a few centimetres in height across the whole bridge to keep the water's fall gentle and even.

The stones were cut to fit without mortar, some weighing several tonnes, and lifted into place with cranes and scaffolding whose sockets are still visible in the piers. The bridge stopped carrying water by the sixth century as the aqueduct fell out of use, but the structure itself survived intact and is now one of the best preserved Roman aqueduct bridges anywhere.

The true arch, wedge-shaped stones locking together so the load pushes outward and down rather than straight down, was known before Rome. What Roman builders did was work out how to repeat it reliably at scale, in concrete and stone alike, and combine it with their own hydraulic concrete to build structures that did not need a forest of internal columns.

That combination let Roman engineers span far wider gaps than earlier builders could manage safely. Aqueducts carried water across whole valleys on tiers of stacked arches, the Pont du Gard among the most complete survivors, while the same principle let vaulted ceilings roof over public buildings without a single wall carrying weight through the middle.

The Astrodome opened in Houston in April 1965 as the first stadium with a permanent roof over a professional playing field, ending baseball's total dependence on the weather. Judge Roy Hofheinz, who pushed the project through, wanted air conditioning as much as a roof, having sweated through enough Houston summers at the ballpark to think domed comfort would sell tickets on its own.

Real grass died under the dome's translucent panels once outfielders complained the glare made fly balls impossible to track and the panels were painted over, so the club switched to an artificial turf developed for the purpose: AstroTurf, named for the building. The Astrodome was nicknamed the Eighth Wonder of the World at its opening and stopped hosting a professional team by 2000, replaced by newer stadiums with retractable roofs.

Egypt finished the Aswan High Dam in 1970 after eleven years of construction with heavy Soviet financing and engineering, after the United States and Britain withdrew an earlier funding offer amid Cold War manoeuvring over the Suez Canal. The dam ended the Nile's annual flood cycle that Egyptian farming had depended on for thousands of years, trading unpredictable flooding for controlled irrigation and year-round electricity.

Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, flooded ancient Nubian land and forced the relocation of roughly 100,000 people, and prompted an international campaign that cut apart and moved the temples of Abu Simbel to keep them above the new waterline. The dam ended catastrophic Nile flooding but also trapped the silt that had fertilised Egyptian fields for millennia, a trade that farmers are still adjusting to.

Philip Johnson had spent decades as modernism's champion, co-curating the 1932 show that named the International Style, before designing a skyscraper that broke almost every rule of it. The broken pediment on top, split open like a piece of furniture, made the building an instant argument starter in a city still built on glass boxes.

AT&T sold the tower in 1993 as the phone giant restructured, and Sony took it over as its US headquarters, adding a Sony sign to the crown. It later passed to 550 Madison Avenue's owners and was reworked with a glass base by Snohetta, though the granite Chippendale top that made it famous was left alone.

The network Hitler championed as a civilian marvel was planned from the start with military logistics in mind. Construction relied increasingly on forced labour once the war began, including concentration camp prisoners, as the workforce needed to keep laying concrete competed directly with the army for men.

By 1942 around 3,800 kilometres, roughly 2,360 miles, had been completed against a planned network of over 20,000 kilometres. Wartime shortages of steel, fuel and workers had already stalled most new construction, and the unfinished autobahn plan was never resumed at anything like its original scale after the war.

Karl Benz filed his patent for the Benz Patent-Motorwagen in January 1886, a three-wheeled carriage powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. It is usually credited as the first vehicle built from the ground up as an automobile rather than a converted horse carriage, though other inventors in Germany and France were experimenting with motorised carriages around the same years.

The Motorwagen only became famous after Benz's wife, Bertha, took it on an unauthorised 106-kilometre round trip in 1888 to prove it roadworthy, buying fuel from pharmacies along the way and fixing mechanical faults herself. Her drive is often credited with the machine's first real publicity and with proving cars could travel real distances.

Bactria sat where the Hindu Kush meets Central Asia's river valleys, a region Alexander's successors held long after his empire split apart. Greek rulers there minted coins with Greek gods on one face and, later, Buddhist imagery on the other, a mixing of traditions visible nowhere else on this scale.

Caravans moving between Han China, India and the Mediterranean had to pass through Bactrian territory, and Greco-Bactrian kings taxed and protected that traffic rather than producing much for export themselves. The kingdom fragmented under pressure from nomadic groups migrating out of the steppe during the second century BCE, but the routes through it kept operating under new rulers.

I.M. Pei designed the tower as four triangular shafts of unequal height rising from a square base, a shape chosen partly to shed wind loads without the internal steel bracing a conventional skyscraper of that height would need. Its diagonal crisscross bracing is visible through the glass skin rather than hidden inside it.

The building's sharp angles and its feng shui implications drew immediate controversy in Hong Kong, where nearby property owners complained the tower's edges pointed at their offices like knives. Pei's own father had worked for the Bank of China decades earlier, and the finished tower briefly ranked as the tallest building outside the United States.

The complex covered around 25 hectares and could hold several thousand bathers at once, moving through cold, warm and hot rooms heated by furnaces tended by slaves in tunnels beneath the floors. Its libraries, gardens and exercise grounds made it a social venue as much as a place to wash, funded largely by wealth Caracalla extracted through a tax that extended Roman citizenship to nearly all free provincials.

It stayed in use for roughly three centuries until invading Ostrogoths cut Rome's aqueducts in 537, ending the water supply the baths depended on. The ruins later became a quarry for building stone and, in the twentieth century, an outdoor opera stage among the surviving brick vaults.

Long before couriers or written despatches could cross a region, hilltop fires relayed a single piece of information fast: an enemy fleet sighted, a city fallen, a signal expected on a given night. Aeschylus has the fall of Troy reach Mycenae this way in his play Agamemnon, beacon answering beacon across the Aegean, though the play is drama rather than a historical record of the event.

The method carried almost no detail beyond a prearranged yes or no, since a fire either burned or did not. Thucydides describes Greek city-states using beacon chains for real military warning during the Peloponnesian War, a much better attested case than Aeschylus's Troy, showing the technique in practical use rather than as a poetic device.

The stadium's lattice of interlocking steel beams, designed with the artist Ai Weiwei working alongside architects Herzog and de Meuron, was meant to look like woven twigs rather than an engineered frame, and the nickname Bird's Nest stuck to it well before it hosted its first event. Ai later distanced himself from the finished project, criticising the way Beijing used the Games around it.

Construction finished in 2008 in time for the Olympic opening ceremony that August, after roughly 42,000 tonnes of steel went into the frame, some of the heaviest steelwork used in any stadium built to that date. It hosted the athletics and both opening and closing ceremonies, then sat under debate for years over how a venue that size should be used once the Games had left.

On the night of 12 to 13 August 1961, East German soldiers strung barbed wire through Berlin along the boundary between the Soviet and Western sectors. Families woke to find streets they had crossed daily suddenly cut in half, some literally: a wall ran down the middle of Bernauer Strasse, splitting buildings from their own front doors. Within days, workers replaced the wire with concrete blocks.

The wall grew into a 155-kilometre barrier with guard towers, dog runs and a mined strip East Germans called the death zone. At least 140 people died trying to cross it over the next 28 years. It fell not by demolition order but by confusion: on 9 November 1989 a mis-relayed announcement let crowds through the checkpoints that night, and the guards simply stood aside.

Norman Foster's studio designed the Bilbao Metro's above-ground entrances as curved glass and steel canopies that locals nicknamed fosteritos, a rare case of a transit system's hardware becoming a recognisable civic symbol rather than street furniture people ignore. The system opened as part of a wider push to rebuild Bilbao's economy after its steel and shipbuilding industries collapsed through the 1980s.

The metro predates the Guggenheim Bilbao by two years, and both projects are usually credited together with turning a declining industrial port into a case study cities elsewhere tried to copy, a pattern that came to be called the Bilbao effect. Foster's firm designed the stations' interiors as well, using the same rounded, tunnel-like vaulting throughout.

Borobudur was raised on Java by the Sailendra dynasty between roughly 750 and 842, using about 60,000 cubic metres of volcanic stone stacked without mortar into nine terraces, six square and three circular, that visitors climb as a walking path through carved scenes of Buddhist teaching.

It remains the largest Buddhist monument on earth, but it was not permanently in use for long: volcanic ash and jungle growth buried it after Islam displaced Buddhism as Java's dominant religion, and it stayed hidden until the British administrator Thomas Stamford Raffles had it cleared in 1814.

President Juscelino Kubitschek staked his term on building an entirely new capital from empty savanna, fulfilling a promise written into Brazil's 1891 constitution but never acted on. Urban planner Lucio Costa laid the city out in the shape of an aeroplane or a bow, and Oscar Niemeyer designed its curving government buildings, working to a deadline Kubitschek refused to let slip.

Brasilia was inaugurated on 21 April 1960, after roughly three years of construction rather than the four sometimes claimed, built largely by migrant labourers housed in makeshift camps that became satellite towns once the capital was finished. UNESCO later listed its modernist core as a World Heritage Site.

Four private companies, grouped together only since 1923 out of over a hundred smaller ones, passed into state hands on 1 January 1948 under the Transport Act 1945's nationalisation programme. Decades of underinvestment and wartime damage had left the network in poor shape, and the postwar Labour government argued that only public ownership could fund its recovery.

British Railways ran the system for nearly half a century, surviving the deep cuts of the 1960s Beeching reports that closed thousands of miles of track. Privatisation began in 1994 and split the network into competing operating companies, reversing the 1948 settlement rather than restoring the pre nationalisation companies.

Construction on the East River span began in January 1869, months before the design's engineer, John A. Roebling, even set foot on the site again: he died weeks later of tetanus after a foot injury sustained surveying the route. His son Washington Roebling took over as chief engineer and pushed the project through for the next fourteen years.

Building the towers required men to work inside pressurised wooden caissons sunk to bedrock beneath the riverbed, where the air pressure caused what workers called caisson disease, now known as decompression sickness. Washington Roebling himself was left partially paralysed by it, directing later stages of the work from a nearby apartment using a telescope.

The bridge opened on 24 May 1883, fourteen years after ground was broken and the design's original engineer, John A. Roebling, had died of an infection from a survey accident. His son Washington Roebling finished the project, watching the opening ceremony from his window because decompression sickness suffered during the caisson work had left him too disabled to attend in person.

Six days after opening, a stairway crush killed twelve people after a rumour spread that the bridge was collapsing under the crowd's weight. To prove the structure sound, showman P.T. Barnum led a herd of twenty-one elephants across it the following year, an event that did more to reassure the public than any engineering report.

The building on the site in 1703 was not a palace at all but Buckingham House, a red brick townhouse built for the Duke of Buckingham as a private residence. It stood well back from St James's Park on ground once used as a mulberry garden by James I, who had hoped, unsuccessfully, to grow silk there.

George III bought the house in 1761 as a family retreat away from the formality of St James's Palace, and it only began turning into today's palace when John Nash remodelled it for George IV in the 1820s. It did not become the monarch's official London residence until Queen Victoria moved in after 1837.

Bukhara's rise as a Silk Road hub had older roots, but it was under the Samanid dynasty, from the late 9th century, that the city became the capital of a Persian-speaking state wealthy enough to fund one of the era's great libraries, drawing scholars including the young Ibn Sina, later known in the West as Avicenna.

Merchants passing through carried goods between China, India and the Islamic Mediterranean, and the city's wealth was built as much on that transit trade, and on taxing it, as on anything Bukhara produced itself, a pattern common to the Silk Road's great inland cities.

A small temple had stood on the site since 528, but the Bulguksa known today began in 751 under the Silla chief minister Kim Daeseong, who is said to have commissioned it to honour his parents. He died before it was finished, and the Silla court completed the work in 774.

Its granite terraces and the twin pagodas Seokgatap and Dabotap survived largely intact because they were built of stone rather than the wood used for the halls above them, which burned during a Japanese invasion in the 1590s and had to be rebuilt afterward.

The hotel is built on an artificial island 280 metres offshore, connected to the mainland by a private curving causeway, because Dubai's ruler wanted a structure isolated enough that its silhouette against the Gulf would never be crowded by a neighbour. The sail-like frame is a steel exoskeleton wrapped around a concrete tower, with the open front face covered in a Teflon-coated fibreglass membrane rather than glass.

Inside, the atrium rises the full height of the building, and every one of the roughly 200 units is a two-storey suite rather than a single room, so the hotel's true room count is far smaller than its size suggests. It opened in December 1999 and was marketed as a seven-star property, a rating no official body issues, though the phrase has stuck to it ever since.

The tower opened on 4 January 2010 at 828 metres, a height its developers kept secret until the ribbon-cutting ceremony itself to prevent rival projects from redesigning around it. It was renamed days before opening, from Burj Dubai to Burj Khalifa, honouring the president of the United Arab Emirates after Abu Dhabi provided financial support during Dubai's debt crisis.

Its Y-shaped floor plan, tapering in setbacks as it rises, was engineered specifically to disrupt wind vortices that would otherwise sway a tower this tall. It overtook Taipei 101 as the world's tallest building and has held the title since, with the elevators alone, among the fastest in the world, needed to move people through more than 160 occupied floors.

Hagia Sophia, finished in 537 under Justinian I, is the reason 550 gets treated as a peak: its dome, 31 metres across and seemingly weightless, was carried on pendentives, a curved masonry solution that let architects Anthemius and Isidore set a circular dome over a square floor plan for the first time at that scale.

The technique spread with imperial money rather than staying a one-off. Domed basilicas modelled on that solution went up from Ravenna to the Balkans over the following decades, and the pendentive dome became the standard vocabulary of Orthodox church building for the next thousand years.

Horses and donkeys cannot cross the Sahara; a camel can go roughly two weeks without drinking. That single fact, not any single ruler or battle, is what opened the desert to sustained trade, as camel use spread among Berber traders in the early centuries CE and turned a barrier into a route.

Caravans of hundreds of camels began moving West African gold and salt north to Mediterranean markets, with enslaved people traded along the same routes. The camel did not replace an older desert trade; before it, there had been almost none, because no other animal could make the crossing survive it.

The last spike was driven at Craigellachie, British Columbia, on 7 November 1885, completing a rail line promised to British Columbia as a condition of its joining Confederation in 1871. Thousands of Chinese labourers, paid far less than white workers and given the most dangerous blasting work through the Rockies, died in numbers that were never properly recorded.

The railway bound a country over 4,600 kilometres wide into a single transport network and let Ottawa move troops west within days to suppress the North-West Rebellion the same year construction reached its final stretch. It remains one of the largest engineering undertakings attempted by a country of Canada's population at the time.

Venice was not planned around its canals so much as built into a lagoon that left no other option. Its buildings sit on timber piles driven through mud into firmer clay below, and the waterways between them, the Grand Canal chief among them, doubled as the city's streets long before any road network existed.

By the eleventh century that lagoon geography had become an advantage rather than a limitation. Venetian ships could load and unload directly against a merchant's own doorstep, and the canal network let the city grow into a hub of Adriatic and eastern Mediterranean trade without ever needing to compete for overland routes.

One Canada Square rose on derelict docklands that had emptied out through the 1960s and 1970s as container shipping moved cargo handling elsewhere, leaving the Isle of Dogs one of London's poorest areas. Its developer, Olympia and York, went into administration in 1992 not long after the tower opened, a casualty of the same property crash that had also hit its owner's other projects in New York.

The tower held the title of the UK's tallest building for over a decade, until the Shard overtook it in 2012 and Canary Wharf's own later neighbours, including One Canada Square's taller successors nearby, pushed it further down the list. Its pyramid-capped top, lit at night, became the skyline marker for a district that took most of the 1990s to fill with tenants.

Before anyone called it the Silk Road, Central Asian oasis towns were already linked by caravan routes carrying goods between settled agricultural regions and the steppe. By the fifth century BCE these paths connected places like Samarkand and Bukhara, watering points that made a multi-week desert crossing survivable for pack animals and traders alike.

Those routes existed because geography forced them into a narrow set of paths: mountain passes, river valleys and strings of oases were the only viable crossings of an otherwise punishing terrain. When Chinese silk began moving west in bulk under the Han dynasty a few centuries later, it travelled along a network that Central Asian traders had already worn into the landscape.

Catalhoyuk, on the Anatolian plain in modern Turkey, had no streets. Houses were packed wall to wall and entered through holes in the roof, so residents walked across their neighbours' ceilings to get home. At its height the settlement held several thousand people across a mound built up over centuries of houses rebuilt on top of older ones.

Excavated from 1961 onward, the site shows no clear temples, palaces or ruling elite, an arrangement that unsettled earlier assumptions about how cities begin. Burials placed under the floors of the very houses people lived in suggest the dead stayed close to the living rather than being set apart in a separate ground.

A French monk named Rodulfus Glaber wrote that after the year 1000, it was as if the world had shaken itself and cast off its old age to be clothed everywhere in a white mantle of churches. His words describe a real building surge across Western Europe, driven by growing towns, more settled political conditions and church wealth flowing into stone.

The style that resulted, Romanesque, favoured thick walls, round arches and small windows because builders had not yet solved how to support tall stone vaults on slender supports. That problem would not be answered until Gothic ribbed vaulting and flying buttresses arrived in the following century, letting walls open up into the glass that Romanesque churches could not carry.

Empress Elizabeth had the Italian architect Bartolomeo Rastrelli rebuild her mother Catherine I's earlier residence at Tsarskoye Selo into a vast baroque palace, finished in 1756 with a facade stretching some 325 metres and reportedly gilded with over 100 kilograms of gold leaf. Elizabeth had grown dissatisfied with the earlier, smaller building and demanded something to rival Versailles.

Its most famous room, the Amber Room, was lined with panels gifted to Peter the Great by the Prussian king in 1716 and later installed here. German forces dismantled and removed the room during the Second World War occupation of the palace, and it has never been recovered; a reconstructed replica now stands in its place.

The Large Hadron Collider occupies a tunnel 27 kilometres in circumference, built in the 1980s for CERN's earlier LEP collider and reused rather than dug fresh, straddling the border between Switzerland and France roughly 100 metres underground. Its magnets have to be cooled with liquid helium to below 2 kelvin, colder than deep space, to stay superconducting at the currents needed to bend proton beams around the ring.

Construction and installation finished in 2008, and the collider was switched on that September, only to suffer a faulty electrical connection nine days later that melted magnets and shut it down for over a year of repairs. It resumed in 2009 and by 2012 had produced the data used to confirm the Higgs boson, the discovery the machine had largely been built to chase.

By the 1070s Chaco Canyon's great houses had grown well beyond simple residences, multi-story masonry buildings with thick, precisely coursed walls rising several storeys around large open plazas. Pueblo Bonito, Chetro Ketl and their neighbours show a level of planning, aligned walls, standardised room sizes, that points to organised labour rather than piecemeal growth.

Few of these rooms show signs of everyday habitation such as hearths or worn floors, which has led archaeologists to read the great houses as ceremonial and administrative centres serving communities scattered across the wider San Juan Basin, tied together by the road network radiating out from the canyon.

The roads radiating out from Chaco Canyon were built wider and straighter than travel alone required, some running nine metres across, cut through rock and banked over dips rather than following the easiest ground. Several stretch for tens of kilometres in an almost perfectly straight line toward outlying great houses across the San Juan Basin.

Wheeled transport and pack animals were both absent from this world, which is part of why archaeologists doubt the roads were built purely for moving goods. Many seem oriented toward shrines, other great houses or cardinal directions, suggesting the network carried ceremonial and social meaning for Ancestral Puebloan communities as much as practical traffic.

Engineers had proposed a tunnel under the Channel since Napoleon's era, and a short section was actually bored from the French side in the 1880s before British military fears of invasion shut it down. The 1988 start followed a 1986 treaty between Margaret Thatcher and Francois Mitterrand and was funded entirely by private capital, with no government money in the construction.

Boring machines started from both Folkestone and Sangatte, cutting through chalk marl chosen because it is watertight and easy to excavate. The private financing structure later strained badly: Eurotunnel needed multiple debt restructurings in the 1990s and 2000s, since the tunnel cost roughly double its original budget.

Francis I ordered Chambord built mainly as a hunting lodge near a forest he already favoured, yet the result outgrew that purpose entirely: a double-helix staircase, hundreds of rooms and a skyline of towers and chimneys that made the roofline look like a small town. Construction ran from 1519 and the main structure was largely finished by 1547, though decoration continued afterward.

Francis rarely stayed there, reportedly visiting only a handful of times in total, since the surrounding marshland made the chateau cold and hard to keep supplied. Leonardo da Vinci, then working for Francis, is often credited with influencing the design, though no signed plan by him survives to confirm it.

El Castillo, the stepped pyramid that defines Chichen Itza, was built to double as a calendar: its four staircases total 364 steps, and on the spring and autumn equinoxes, sunlight and shadow crawl along the northern staircase's balustrade in a pattern that looks like a serpent descending.

The city's rise around 1000 CE came from a fusion rarely matched elsewhere in the Maya world, blending Maya building traditions with forms brought or adopted from the Toltecs of central Mexico, visible in the feathered-serpent columns that also appear at Toltec Tula.

China's first dedicated high-speed line ran between Beijing and Tianjin, opening on 1 August 2008 in time to carry spectators to that summer's Olympic events, with trains built to run at up to 350 kilometres per hour over the roughly 120-kilometre route. It was a demonstration line as much as a transport project, timed deliberately to coincide with the Games.

What followed was rapid rather than gradual. Within little more than a decade China had built out a network exceeding any other country's high-speed rail mileage combined, including the Beijing-Shanghai line and the Danyang-Kunshan viaduct, connecting cities across the country at a pace that reshaped domestic travel patterns within a single generation.

The Chrysler Building topped out in 1930 after its architect, William Van Alen, secretly assembled a 38-metre steel spire inside the building's fire shafts and hoisted it into place in under two hours, a stunt aimed squarely at beating a rival tower being built downtown by his former partner. The surprise addition pushed the building past 1,046 feet and past the Eiffel Tower as the tallest structure on earth.

The title lasted less than a year. The Empire State Building opened in May 1931 at 1,250 feet, and Walter Chrysler, who had funded his tower personally rather than through his car company, never got the lasting record he wanted. The building's stainless-steel crown and hubcap-shaped ornaments remain closely tied to its brief reign at the top.

Queen Elizabeth II and President Francois Mitterrand formally opened the tunnel on 6 May 1994, six years after boring began and roughly double the original budget later, making it one of the most expensive infrastructure projects Britain and France had jointly undertaken. Eurostar passenger services and freight shuttles both began running that year.

The tunnel's 38 kilometre undersea section remains the longest of any underwater tunnel in the world, even though Japan's Seikan Tunnel, finished six years earlier, is longer overall and dips deeper below the seabed. A journey that once took a cross-Channel ferry well over an hour could now be made by train in about thirty-five minutes.

Canadian National built the CN Tower in Toronto to solve a practical problem: radio and television signals were bouncing off the city's growing cluster of skyscrapers, garbling reception across the region. Finished in 1976 at 553 metres, it rose well above every building the signals had been bouncing off, and broadcasters mounted their transmitters near its top once it opened.

At completion it was the tallest freestanding structure in the world, a title it held for more than three decades until Dubai's Burj Khalifa overtook it in 2007. The tower's glass floor, added later, sits 342 metres above the ground and is rated to hold the weight of roughly 14 moose, a comparison Canadian engineers apparently found more persuasive than tonnes.

Vespasian broke ground in 72 on marshland where Nero had drained a lake for his private villa gardens. Building on a former emperor's pleasure grounds was a deliberate message: the site was being handed back to Rome as a public arena, paid for with spoils from the recent Jewish War rather than the treasury.

The building held an estimated 50,000 to 87,000 people across four tiers, easily the largest amphitheatre the Roman world built. It kept that title for close to two thousand years; no ancient or medieval structure matched its footprint, and only twentieth century stadiums eventually surpassed its capacity.

Titus opened the finished amphitheatre in 80, a year after his father Vespasian died without seeing it completed. The inaugural games are said to have run for a hundred days, with animal hunts, gladiator combat and staged naval battles flooding the arena floor from a system of underground channels and lifts.

Estimates of capacity range from about 50,000 to 87,000, depending on how tightly the tiered stone seating is packed and whether standing areas count. Either way it was the largest amphitheatre the Roman world produced, a record that held for close to two thousand years before modern stadiums overtook it.

Rhodes built the Colossus around 280 BCE to celebrate surviving a siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes, melting down the besieger's abandoned bronze siege equipment to help fund it. Standing roughly 33 metres tall on an iron and stone frame packed with weights for stability, it was not the leg-straddling harbour statue of later paintings; ancient sources give no evidence it stood over the entrance at all.

An earthquake snapped the statue at the knees around 226 BCE, after it had stood for barely half a century. An Egyptian king offered to pay for its rebuilding, but an oracle reportedly convinced Rhodes the collapse was a sign from the gods, so the bronze remains lay where they fell for centuries, described by later travellers, until they were eventually sold as scrap.

The 12.9 kilometre bridge across the Northumberland Strait ended Prince Edward Island's dependence on ferries and winter ice-breaking boats for its road link to the mainland, a promise the province had been made when it joined Canadian confederation in 1873. Its piers carry cone-shaped ice shields that force the strait's thick winter ice to ride up and break rather than pushing the supports sideways.

It is the longest bridge in the world built over waters that freeze every winter, a title distinct from the world's longest bridge overall, a record China's viaducts hold by a wide margin. Some Islanders opposed the project before it opened in 1997, worried a fixed link would end the sense of separateness a ferry crossing had always given the island.

Constantine chose the Greek town of Byzantium for his new capital because it sat on a strait between Europe and Asia, easy to defend and to supply by sea. He dedicated the rebuilt city in 330, filling it with statues and treasures shipped in from across the empire and renaming it after himself.

The choice split the Roman world in practice long before it split on paper: within decades an eastern and western administration ran separately, and the west collapsed in 476 while Constantinople's empire continued for almost another thousand years. Ottoman forces finally took the city in 1453, ending that continuity.

Justinian handed the job to two teachers of geometry rather than a builder. Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus had written on mirrors, vaults and conic sections but had never raised anything close to this scale, and their dome sat flatter than its supports could safely carry. Earthquakes in 553 and 557 cracked it, and a third quake on the morning of 7 May 558 brought part of it down onto the altar and pulpit.

The repair went to Isidore's nephew, also named Isidore, who rebuilt the dome about six metres taller and added forty ribs to carry its weight down into the piers rather than out into the walls. The work finished in 562, and that steeper, ribbed dome has stood since, propped up over the centuries by buttresses that later Byzantine and Ottoman builders added to keep it up.

The Crimean Bridge opened in May 2018, a pair of parallel spans across the Kerch Strait, one carrying road traffic and one rail, together running about 19 kilometres. Vladimir Putin drove a truck across the road section for its opening, four years after Russia annexed Crimea, the event the bridge was built to make physically permanent.

At 19 kilometres it overtook Portugal's Vasco da Gama Bridge, open since 1998, as the longest bridge in Europe. Ukraine and most Western governments never recognised the bridge as legitimate, treating it as built on annexed territory rather than as an ordinary engineering milestone.

Tunnelling for what became the Elizabeth line began in 2009, after decades of proposals for an east-west rail link under central London had stalled repeatedly over funding. Eight tunnel boring machines, each given a name chosen by public vote, dug twin tunnels roughly 21 kilometres long beneath some of the most heavily built-up ground in Europe, threading between Underground lines, sewers and foundations with centimetres of clearance in places.

The project ran years behind its original schedule and well over its initial budget before the central section finally opened to passengers in 2022. Archaeologists working ahead of the tunnellers recovered remains from a Bronze Age riverbed and a mass burial site near Liverpool Street linked to the seventeenth-century plague.

The Elizabeth Line opened in May 2022, over three years later than its original December 2018 target, after tunnelling problems and a fit-out crisis in its central stations forced repeated delays. Queen Elizabeth II, for whom it was named, attended the opening in one of her last public appearances before her death that September.

It runs roughly 100 kilometres from Reading and Heathrow in the west to Essex in the east, threading 42 kilometres of new tunnel beneath central London. It was built as the Crossrail project and renamed on opening, and it became the busiest railway in Britain within its first year.

Wootz steel was first produced in southern India around 300 BCE, its name a corruption of ukku, a Tamil and Telugu word for steel. Metalworkers sealed iron with wood chips and other carbon-rich material in sealed clay crucibles and heated the mixture until it partially melted, letting carbon distribute evenly through the metal.

The resulting high-carbon steel could hold a sharper edge than ordinary wrought iron and was exported west for centuries, reaching Persia and the Middle East long before Europe had an equivalent process. Bladesmiths in Damascus forged imported wootz ingots into weapons prized for their surface pattern, though the steel itself had already been made in India before it ever reached them.

Joseph Paxton designed the Crystal Palace in barely ten days, drawing on his experience building glasshouses for the Duke of Devonshire, and it went up in London's Hyde Park in under six months using prefabricated cast iron and nearly 300,000 panes of glass. It opened in May 1851 to house the Great Exhibition, the first international fair of industry and manufacturing.

Six million visitors, roughly a third of Britain's population at the time, passed through before it closed that October, drawn by exhibits ranging from the Koh-i-Noor diamond to early machine tools. The building was later moved and re-erected in south London, where it stood until a fire destroyed it in 1936.

The wavy surface pattern that gave Damascus steel its name did not originate in Syria at all. It came from wootz, a high-carbon crucible steel first made in southern India around the third century BCE, where iron and carbon-rich material were sealed in clay containers and heated until the metal absorbed carbon evenly through the melt.

Ingots of wootz travelled west by sea and caravan for centuries, and Damascus became known for the swords forged from imported ukku steel rather than for smelting it locally. The banding pattern comes from carbide structures that form as the ingot cools slowly, a process blacksmiths could exploit but not fully explain until modern metallurgy examined it.

The bridge carries the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed railway across roughly 164 kilometres of the Yangtze River delta, much of it over paddy fields, lakes and canals rather than a single wide waterway, which is why a viaduct rather than a conventional single-span bridge made sense here. Around 10,000 workers built it in about four years, finishing in 2010 ahead of the line's opening in 2011.

By length it is the longest bridge in the world, well ahead of any bridge built before it, a record set by stitching together thousands of prefabricated concrete sections rather than by any single dramatic span. Its scale reflects the flood-prone, waterlogged terrain of the delta more than any ambition to set a record on its own.

The first stretch of the Delhi Metro, an elevated line running from Shahdara to Tis Hazari, opened on 24 December 2002. It ran on the surface and above ground for its early years; the network's first underground section did not open until December 2004, and only then did Delhi's system formally overtake the older Kolkata Metro, which had been running since 1984, as the busier of the two.

Delhi's network grew far beyond that first line. It now carries several million riders a day across colour-coded lines stretching close to 400 kilometres, making it one of the largest metro systems in the world by route length, a scale nobody planning the 2002 opening had reason to expect from a single elevated stretch.

Denver International replaced the cramped Stapleton Airport, and opened sixteen months late and roughly two billion dollars over budget, largely because of a fully automated baggage system that never worked reliably and was mostly abandoned within years. The white tension-fabric roof, evoking Rocky Mountain peaks, became the building's identity despite the troubled rollout underneath it.

At over 135 square kilometres, the airport's site is larger than the city of Denver's own downtown many times over, giving it room for runways long enough to handle fully loaded jets even at its mile-high elevation, where thinner air demands extra takeoff distance. Persistent conspiracy theories about tunnels beneath the terminal have followed the airport for decades, fed largely by its remote size and unusual artwork.

The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik completed the shrine in 691 on the Temple Mount, a site holy to Jews, Christians and Muslims alike, over the rock where Islamic tradition holds Muhammad ascended to heaven. Its octagonal plan and mosaic-covered dome borrowed directly from Byzantine church architecture rather than starting from a distinct Islamic template, since none yet existed.

An inscription running inside the building names Abd al-Malik and carries some of the earliest surviving Quranic text, though a later caliph had his own name substituted for the original builder's in one spot, a swap historians only detected centuries afterward by checking the date against known reigns.

A talking drum does not send Morse-style code with an arbitrary signal. West and Central African drummers imitated the tones and rhythms of spoken language itself, since many of the region's languages are tonal, so a skilled drummer could reproduce a phrase's pitch pattern closely enough for a listener to recognise the words.

That let messages carry over distances a shout never could, drum relayed to drum through dense forest where sightlines were useless. European travellers who encountered the practice in the nineteenth century often mistook it for a simple alarm signal, missing that it was closer to a spoken sentence played on an instrument than a code in the cryptographic sense.

Gustave Eiffel's tower was completed in March 1889 as the centrepiece of that year's Paris World's Fair, and it was only meant to stand for twenty years before demolition. It survived because Eiffel had fitted it with a radio antenna and pitched its usefulness for military communication and weather observation, arguments that persuaded the city to keep it standing after the permit expired.

At 300 metres it was the tallest structure in the world when it opened, a title it held until New York's Chrysler Building overtook it in 1930. A group of prominent artists and writers had petitioned against building it at all, calling it a monstrous eyesore over Paris, an objection the tower long outlived.

Ellora is not one monument but 34, cut into a single basalt cliff face in Maharashtra from roughly the 6th to the 10th century, with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain excavations standing side by side and, in places, overlapping in date rather than following a tidy sequence.

The site's centrepiece, the Kailasa temple, was not built up from stone but carved downward out of the rockface as one continuous mass, its makers removing an estimated 200,000 tonnes of rock to leave a freestanding temple with no joints and no imported material at all.

The Empire State Building opened on 1 May 1931, just over a year after construction began, a pace made possible by prefabricated steel delivered on a strict daily schedule and a workforce that at points added more than four storeys a week. It overtook the Chrysler Building, completed only eleven months earlier, to become the tallest building on earth at 1,250 feet.

It kept that title for roughly forty years until Manhattan's own World Trade Center overtook it in 1970. For much of the Depression it was known locally as the 'Empty State Building' because so many of its offices sat unrented, and its owners leaned on a novel source of income instead: charging tourists to ride to the observation deck.

The 363 mile canal linking Lake Erie at Buffalo to the Hudson River at Albany opened fully in October 1825, after eight years of digging that used no engineers trained in canal building, since none existed yet in the United States. Its 83 locks lifted boats past Niagara's drop in elevation without any need to portage around the falls.

New York state funded the project after Congress and other states declined, and tolls repaid the construction cost within about a decade. Freight rates between the Midwest and the Atlantic coast fell sharply once it opened, and the canal is widely credited with helping make New York City the country's dominant port over rivals like Philadelphia and Baltimore.

Water clocks had existed for centuries by 725, but they drifted, because a steady flow of water is hard to hold constant. Yi Xing, a Buddhist monk and astronomer, and the engineer Liang Lingzan solved that for the Tang court by adding a mechanism that let a wheel advance only in fixed, regulated steps rather than turning freely.

That regulator, an escapement, is the same basic idea that governs a mechanical clock centuries later in Europe, though no direct link between the two has been shown. Their device drove an armillary sphere and a rotating globe modelling the sky, with bells and drums sounding automatically to mark the hours, built for a court concerned with astronomy and calendar-keeping rather than everyday timekeeping.

Philip II commissioned El Escorial partly to fulfil a vow made after a battlefield victory on Saint Lawrence's feast day, and the complex combines a monastery, a royal palace, a library and a mausoleum for Spanish monarchs in one severe granite building outside Madrid. Construction ran from 1563 and was completed in 1584, though Philip kept adding to its library and art collection afterward.

Philip governed much of his empire from a small, plainly furnished room there with a direct view into the church, choosing austerity over the ornament typical of royal residences elsewhere in Europe. Spanish monarchs have been buried in its crypt since his own death in 1598.

On 1 December 1990, Englishman Graham Fagg and Frenchman Philippe Cozette shook hands through a small hole in the service tunnel, 40 metres beneath the seabed of the English Channel, the first physical link between mainland Britain and continental Europe since the ice age. Television crews on both sides broadcast the moment live.

Boring had started from Folkestone and Sangatte in 1988 using huge rotating cutter heads, and the two drives met within centimetres of their planned line despite running for years without direct contact. The breakthrough came four years before passenger and freight trains actually began running through the finished tunnel in 1994.

Edgar Kaufmann Jr. expected a house with a view of the waterfall on his family's land. Frank Lloyd Wright built the house on top of it instead, cantilevering concrete terraces directly over the falling water so the sound would be part of living there, a decision the family's own engineers warned might not hold.

Those engineers were closer to right than Wright admitted. The cantilevers sagged over the following decades from underbuilt reinforcement, and a 2002 restoration had to add steel supports beneath the terraces to stop further deflection without changing how the house looks from outside.

Edith Farnsworth commissioned a weekend retreat and got a glass box on steel stilts above a flood plain in Plano, Illinois. Mies van der Rohe designed it with almost no interior walls and floor to ceiling glass on every side, an idea he had been refining since the 1920s, finally built full size for a client who could afford to indulge it.

Farnsworth and Mies fell out badly over cost overruns and eventually sued each other; she later called the house unlivable, too hot in summer and too exposed to insects and passers by. The house has flooded repeatedly since, and its owners have had to raise it and its furnishings to protect it from the Fox River.

George Ferris, a bridge engineer, built his wheel for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition in Chicago after organisers challenged American designers to produce something to rival the Eiffel Tower from four years earlier. His wheel stood 80 metres tall, carried 36 wooden cars each holding up to 60 people, and turned on the largest axle forged up to that time.

Around 1.4 million people rode it over the fair's run, each trip lasting about twenty minutes for two full revolutions. Ferris never profited much from the ride; disputes with the exposition's organisers over the fees ate into his earnings, and the original wheel was dismantled and later scrapped after a second fair in St. Louis in 1904.

The Aqua Claudia was begun under Caligula and finished by Claudius in 52 CE, carrying water some 69 kilometres from springs near Subiaco into Rome, most of it underground and only the final stretch raised onto the arches that still stand along the Appian Way. It was one of the four aqueducts the Romans themselves ranked as their finest.

It was not Rome's first aqueduct. That was the Aqua Appia, built in 312 BCE, over three and a half centuries earlier and almost entirely underground for secrecy and protection. The Claudia's raised arcade became the more visible symbol of Roman engineering because so much more of its above-ground structure survived intact.

KDKA, a Westinghouse station in Pittsburgh, began broadcasting on 2 November 1920 from a makeshift studio, reading returns from the Harding-Cox presidential election as they came in by telephone. Announcer Leo Rosenberg stayed on air from eight in the evening until after midnight, to an audience Westinghouse itself estimated at only a few thousand listeners with home receivers.

KDKA had received the first commercial broadcasting license in the United States just days earlier. Westinghouse ran the broadcast partly to sell the radio sets it manufactured, and within two years hundreds of new stations had gone on air across the country chasing the same audience.

The Stockton and Darlington Railway opened in September 1825 to move coal from inland pits to the coast, and it is usually credited as the first public railway to carry general goods and, on that first day, passengers, using steam locomotion rather than horses over its full length. George Stephenson built the line and drove its locomotive, Locomotion No. 1, himself on the opening run.

Passenger service was at first an afterthought, carried in a horse-drawn coach called the Experiment rather than by steam, and much of the early traffic was still coal wagons. The line's success persuaded backers to fund the Liverpool and Manchester Railway five years later, which is usually credited as the first railway built for passengers from the outset.

Rome's Forum sat on marshland before the Cloaca Maxima existed. Work began around 600 BCE under Tarquinius Priscus, lining an existing stream bed with stone to carry floodwater and drainage away from the valley, and the last of the Roman kings, Tarquinius Superbus, finished the job.

It started as an open channel and was only vaulted over in stone, section by section, from the 3rd century BCE onward, centuries after the original digging. Parts of that vaulted channel still carry rainwater out of central Rome today, under streets laid long after the empire that built it.

Completed in 1902 on a triangular plot where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue, the Fuller Company's building was nicknamed for its resemblance to a cast-iron clothes iron and the name eventually replaced its formal one. At 22 storeys it was among the tallest buildings in New York at the time, though far from the tallest in the world, and its steel frame was clad in limestone and terracotta rather than masonry that carried the weight.

The narrow prow, only about two metres wide at its point, created unusual wind currents at street level that were said to lift women's skirts, drawing men to loiter nearby until police reportedly moved them along, supposedly the origin of the phrase '23 skidoo' referencing the building's address.

Eero Saarinen won the 1947 competition to design a monument on St Louis's riverfront with a catenary arch, the shape a chain takes hanging freely, inverted. Construction did not finish until October 1965, four years after Saarinen died, leaving him another building he never saw completed. At 192 metres it is the tallest arch structure in the world.

Workers assembled it from stainless steel sections lifted by a pair of custom creeper cranes that climbed the legs as they rose, meeting at the top on 28 October 1965 with barely a centimetre of gap to spare. A tram system inside each leg still carries visitors up to an observation deck, riding through a structure that has no straight vertical anywhere along its curve.

The Ghana Empire, in the western Sahel and unrelated to the modern country that later took its name, did not mine the gold it grew rich on. It controlled the trade routes where West African gold, dug further south, was exchanged for Saharan salt, taking a cut on both goods as they passed through its markets.

Arab geographers writing from the 9th century described its ruler taxing every load of salt entering the kingdom and every load of gold leaving it, a toll system rather than direct production that made Ghana wealthy on the movement of other people's goods.

The Globe was built in 1599 on the south bank of the Thames after the Lord Chamberlain's Men lost the lease on their previous playhouse, the Theatre, in Shoreditch. Rather than abandon the building, they dismantled its timber frame overnight and carried the wood across the frozen river to Southwark to rebuild it as the Globe.

Shakespeare held a share in the company and in the new theatre itself, an unusual arrangement that let him profit directly from performances rather than only from selling plays. The original burned down in 1613 when a cannon fired during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.

The carved limestone pillars at Gobekli Tepe, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, predate pottery, writing and the wheel. They were raised by people who had not yet domesticated wheat, arranged in circles up to twenty metres across and carved with foxes, scorpions and vultures rather than any obvious deity.

No hearths, houses or middens turned up on the earliest levels, which is why archaeologists call it ceremonial rather than residential. Around 8000 BCE the builders buried the pillars under rubble on purpose, and the hill stayed sealed until excavation began in 1995, preserving carving detail a settled village would not have kept.

Chief engineer Joseph Strauss insisted on a safety net slung beneath the deck, an unusual precaution for the time that is credited with saving nineteen men who fell during construction; they called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club. Eleven other workers died on the project, ten of them in a single scaffold collapse in 1937.

The colour was never meant to be permanent. The steel arrived from the fabricator coated in a burnt orange sealant, and the consulting architect Irving Morrow chose to keep that shade, now called international orange, over the US Navy's preferred stripes of black and yellow for visibility in fog.

Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh guru, began building the Harmandir Sahib in 1585 at the centre of a sacred pool, deliberately setting entrances on all four sides so that people of any background could enter without favouring one direction over another. He completed the Adi Granth, the compiled Sikh scriptures, and installed it inside the temple in 1604.

Its gold covering came much later: Maharaja Ranjit Singh had the upper floors gilded with gold leaf in the early nineteenth century, giving the temple the appearance that earned its common English name. The site has since been rebuilt more than once after periods of destruction, including an assault by Mughal and later colonial forces.

The Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in June 2016 after seventeen years of boring beneath the Swiss Alps, running 57 kilometres between Erstfeld and Bodio in two parallel single-track bores. At its deepest point the rock overhead is about 2,300 metres thick, making it the deepest railway tunnel as well as the longest.

It replaced the older Gotthard rail line's steep switchback route with a flat, level path, cutting travel time between Zurich and Milan and letting freight trains cross the Alps without the extra locomotives the old grades demanded. It forms the centrepiece of a rail link planned to run from Rotterdam to Genoa.

Sections of canal linking China's river systems already existed, but Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty ordered them joined and extended between 604 and 609, digging new stretches such as the Tongji Canal to connect the Yellow River valley to the Yangtze and on to Hangzhou. The finished network ran well over a thousand kilometres, letting grain move by barge between north and south China instead of overland.

The project was built largely by conscripted labour under brutal conditions, and the expense helped bring down the Sui dynasty within a decade of completion. Later dynasties kept extending and repairing it, and the Grand Canal remains the longest artificial waterway still in use anywhere in the world.

The Great Belt fixed link actually splits road and rail onto different structures: a suspension bridge with the world's second-longest main span carries road traffic across the eastern channel, while trains cross the same stretch through a bored tunnel, and only the western box-girder bridge, between Zealand and Sprogo, carries both together. It replaced ferries that had linked Denmark's two largest land masses for generations.

Completed in stages through the 1990s and fully open by 1998, the crossing cut a journey that once needed an hour-long ferry down to about ten minutes by car or train. Denmark financed the whole link through tolls and state-backed loans rather than general taxation, a model since copied for the Oresund Bridge to Sweden.

Abd al-Rahman I began the mosque in 785 on the site of a former church, and successive rulers kept enlarging it for two centuries, adding rows of double-tiered horseshoe arches on reused Roman and Visigothic columns. The final expansion under al-Hakam II and his successors, finished around 987, brought the building to roughly 23,000 square metres, one of the largest mosques ever built.

After Christian forces retook Cordoba in 1236 the building became a cathedral, and in the sixteenth century a Renaissance nave was inserted directly into the middle of the forest of arches. Charles V, who authorised the change, reportedly regretted it once he saw the result, saying the builders had destroyed something unique to build something ordinary.

Workers on the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad walked out at Martinsburg, West Virginia, in July 1877 after the company cut wages for the second time that year, its earnings squeezed by a depression that had run since the Panic of 1873. The strike spread along the rail lines within days, reaching Baltimore, Pittsburgh, Chicago and St Louis without any central organisation directing it.

State militias and, eventually, federal troops sent by President Rutherford Hayes broke the strike within about six weeks, with dozens of workers killed in clashes in Pittsburgh and elsewhere. It was the first work stoppage to shut down rail traffic across much of the country, and it pushed later labour organisers toward building unions that could coordinate rather than rely on spontaneous walkouts.

China already had several regional walls before this. Around 220 BCE, Qin Shi Huang, having just unified the warring states, ordered those separate fortifications joined and extended into one continuous defensive line against raids from nomadic peoples to the north, running from Gansu in the west toward Liaodong in the east.

Almost nothing of that Qin-era wall survives; it was built largely of packed earth, and forced labour under harsh conditions killed workers in numbers no reliable count records. The stone and brick wall tourists visit near Beijing today is mostly Ming dynasty work from the 14th to 17th centuries, built more than 1,500 years later on a different line.

Builders working from around 1100 stacked granite blocks into massive walls without mortar, shaping them so precisely that the largest enclosure's curved wall still stands over 10 metres high. The site grew into the capital of a trading kingdom that dealt in gold and ivory reaching as far as China, evidenced by imported porcelain found among the ruins.

Colonial-era archaeologists, reluctant to credit an African society with the site, spent decades attributing it to Phoenicians or other outsiders despite local evidence to the contrary. That claim was abandoned once proper excavation confirmed a Bantu-speaking builders' origin, and the country later named itself after the ruins at independence in 1980.

Frank Gehry clad the museum in titanium panels rather than steel, a material he chose partly because it was, at the time, cheaper than expected after the price collapsed following the end of the Cold War's demand for it in aerospace. The curving forms were only feasible to build because Gehry's team used aircraft-design software, CATIA, to translate his crumpled paper models into buildable steel frames.

The museum's success in reviving a city hit hard by deindustrialisation gave the term Bilbao effect to the idea that a single striking building could revive a declining place, though later attempts elsewhere to replicate it with a landmark museum alone mostly failed. Within a few years of opening, the Guggenheim was drawing roughly a million visitors annually to a city few tourists had previously bothered to visit.

Gwadar sits on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast, close to the Iranian border and far from any rail or major road network, which is precisely why it was chosen: a deep-water port there could bypass the long sea route around India and give landlocked western China a shorter path to open ocean. China financed and built the first phase, largely complete by 2007, well before the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor gave the port its strategic profile.

Construction proceeded slowly relative to the ambitions attached to it. Roads and a planned rail link connecting Gwadar to the rest of Pakistan lagged the port itself for years, and the surrounding town remained small and underdeveloped even as officials described the site as a future hub for regional trade.

Hadrian ordered the wall in 122 after visiting the province himself, and building took at least six years across a workforce drawn from three legions. It ran 73 miles from the Tyne to the Solway Firth, built of stone for the eastern 45 miles and turf in the west, where local stone was scarcer.

The wall was never a simple barrier: forts, milecastles and turrets every third of a mile controlled movement and collected tolls on people crossing rather than sealing the frontier shut. Rome abandoned it as a functioning boundary in the early fifth century, and much of its stone was later quarried by local builders, leaving the low, patchy ruin visible today.

The wall ran about 117 kilometres from coast to coast, built mostly by soldiers of three Roman legions rather than slave labour, with a fort or milecastle at regular intervals along its length. It never marked the true edge of Roman Britain: garrisons and roads pushed further north at times, and the wall functioned more as a controlled, taxable crossing point than a hard frontier.

Within a generation the Antonine Wall was built further north in Scotland, only to be abandoned again within about twenty years, after which Hadrian's Wall resumed its role. Large stretches survive because later builders quarried it for stone, leaving the best-preserved sections in its less accessible middle stretch.

No trace of a garden has ever turned up at Babylon, and the hundreds of surviving building inscriptions of Nebuchadnezzar II, who is credited with the gardens, never mention one. What does survive is an Assyrian relief from Nineveh showing trees on raised terraces, watered by an aqueduct the king Sennacherib boasted of building decades earlier.

That has led a number of historians to argue the wonder belongs to Sennacherib's Nineveh, roughly 550 kilometres north of Babylon, and that Greek writers, working centuries later and at second hand, simply attached the story to the wrong capital and the wrong king.

The airport sits on Chek Lap Kok, an island flattened and extended with reclaimed land to make room for two parallel runways, after Hong Kong's old Kai Tak airport had become notorious for a landing approach that took jets low over apartment blocks. Building it required moving hundreds of millions of cubic metres of fill, one of the largest earthworks in Asia at the time.

Norman Foster's terminal opened in July 1998, only months before a chaotic first few days in which baggage systems and cargo handling briefly broke down under the switch from Kai Tak. Within a few years it had become one of the world's busiest airports for both passengers and air cargo, helped by a purpose-built rail and bridge link into central Hong Kong.

The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau Bridge opened in October 2018, a 55 kilometre crossing of the Pearl River Delta made up of cable-stayed bridge sections, an undersea tunnel, and two artificial islands where the road dips beneath shipping lanes. It cut the road journey between Hong Kong and Zhuhai from about three hours to roughly thirty minutes.

At 55 kilometres it became the longest sea crossing in the world, well ahead of Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway, which is longer overall but crosses freshwater rather than open sea. Construction spanned nine years and required reinforcing the structure against the region's typhoons.

Workers poured the concrete in interlocking columns rather than one continuous mass, because a solid block that size would have taken over a century to cool without cracking. Refrigeration pipes ran through the mix to draw the heat out artificially, and the dam still finished two years ahead of its contracted schedule in 1936.

It was called Boulder Dam for most of its construction, a compromise name after Herbert Hoover's own administration had proposed honouring him and his successor's administration objected. Congress restored the name Hoover in 1947. At 221 metres it was the tallest dam in the world when finished, a record other dams eventually surpassed.

Hopewell communities in the Ohio valley left no writing, but the materials buried in their earthwork mounds trace trade lines across most of the continent. Obsidian came from what is now Yellowstone, copper from the Great Lakes, mica from the southern Appalachians, and shells from the Gulf coast, all carried overland or by river far beyond any single group's own territory.

None of this required a state or standing merchants; goods likely passed hand to hand between neighbouring groups over long distances rather than through direct long journeys. What survives is almost entirely what was placed in burial mounds, so archaeologists are reconstructing a continent-wide network from what people chose to bury with their dead.

The Humber Bridge opened in 1981 between Hessle and Barton-upon-Humber in England, closing a gap that had forced drivers on either bank into a long detour or a ferry crossing. Its main span of 1,410 metres made it the longest single-span suspension bridge in the world, a project that had taken 24 years from parliamentary approval to opening as funding repeatedly stalled.

Like the Verrazzano-Narrows before it, the Humber's two towers had to be built slightly out of parallel, roughly 36 millimetres further apart at their tops than their bases, to account for the earth's curvature over that distance. The bridge held its world record for 16 years until Denmark's Great Belt Bridge overtook it in 1997, and it now ranks well outside the top ten.

Frankincense is dried resin tapped from Boswellia trees that grow best in the harsh, arid stretch covering southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, a range narrow enough that supply was always limited. Burned, it produced a fragrant smoke central to temple ritual across Egypt and Mesopotamia, which meant the resin itself became a heavily traded good.

Camel caravans carried it north through the Arabian peninsula long before ships took over the route by sea. Egyptian records describe expeditions to the land the Egyptians called Punt specifically to obtain incense, and by the first millennium BCE whole cities in southern Arabia had grown wealthy on taxing the trade passing through.

On 16 April 1853 a fourteen carriage train hauled by three locomotives named Sahib, Sindh and Sultan carried around 400 passengers roughly 21 miles from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane. The Great Indian Peninsula Railway had built the line, and colonial officials treated the opening as a showpiece of British engineering brought to the subcontinent.

Governor General Lord Dalhousie had pushed hard for Indian railways as tools of trade and troop movement, and this first short line grew within decades into one of the largest rail networks in the world. It also created a new kind of workforce, since running steam railways at this scale required training thousands of Indian engineers, drivers and clerks almost from nothing.

Assembly began on 20 November 1998 when a Russian Proton rocket launched the Zarya control module, funded and built by Russia but paid for by NASA, an arrangement born out of Cold War rivals suddenly needing each other's hardware. The American Unity module joined it two weeks later, launched on the Space Shuttle Endeavour and bolted on by astronauts during a spacewalk.

What began as two modules grew over more than a decade into a structure the length of a football pitch, assembled from pieces built in the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada and launched on rockets and shuttles from three different countries. It has been continuously occupied since November 2000, longer than any spacecraft before it.

Eisenhower had driven with a military convoy across the country in 1919, a trip that took over two months on roads that kept breaking trucks and axles, and later saw Germany's autobahns during the war. Both experiences fed into the case for a national highway network he pushed through Congress with the Federal Aid Highway Act of 1956.

The act paid 90 percent of construction costs from a new highway trust fund financed by fuel taxes, an arrangement that let states build far faster than they could alone. The network eventually ran to over 40,000 miles, reshaping American commuting, freight and the layout of cities it bypassed.

Cast by Abraham Darby III at his family's Coalbrookdale ironworks and designed with the architect Thomas Pritchard, the bridge opened to traffic on 1 January 1781, spanning the Severn gorge with roughly 378 tons of iron in a single arch over 100 feet across. It let barge traffic pass beneath uninterrupted, something a timber or stone bridge of that span could not have managed.

Its joints copied carpentry techniques, dovetails and wedges, because nobody had cast a structure this large before and iron bridge design had no precedent to follow. The bridge nearly bankrupted the Darby family despite its engineering success, and the small riverside settlement that grew up around it took the bridge's own name, becoming the town of Ironbridge.

Nebuchadnezzar II built the Ishtar Gate around 575 BCE as one of eight gates through Babylon's inner walls, facing the processional way used for the New Year festival. Its surface of blue-glazed bricks, moulded into rows of striding lions, bulls and mythical dragons called sirrush, was made by firing glazed tiles individually and assembling them like a relief puzzle.

German archaeologist Robert Koldewey excavated the gate's foundations between 1902 and 1914, and its bricks were shipped to Berlin, where a reconstructed version stands in the Pergamon Museum today. The original site in Iraq now holds only the buried lower courses and a smaller replica built under Saddam Hussein.

Itaipu straddles the Parana River between Brazil and Paraguay, and the two countries split its output evenly by treaty even though Paraguay uses only a fraction of its half, selling the rest to its larger neighbour. Concrete poured for the project would have built five copies of the Itaipu stadium in Rio, and the diverted river channel used during construction ranks among the largest earth-moving efforts on record.

China's Three Gorges Dam overtook Itaipu's installed capacity in the 2000s, but Itaipu still holds the record for total electricity generated in a single year, a title it has traded back and forth with Three Gorges since 2016 depending on rainfall. In some years it alone has supplied around ninety per cent of Paraguay's electricity and a sixth of Brazil's.

Ground was broken in April 2013 on a tower designed to clear 1,008 metres, well past the Burj Khalifa's 828, and become the first building over a kilometre tall. The contractor, Saudi Binladin Group, was caught up in a 2017 corruption purge, and work stalled the following January with the tower stuck at 63 floors.

It sat unfinished for roughly seven years before a new completion contract restarted work in late 2024, aiming for 2028. Its site, Jeddah's northern shore on the Red Sea, was picked so the tower would eventually anchor an entire planned district around it, not just a skyline.

Cherry trees had to be moved to clear the site, and the women who had campaigned to plant them chained themselves to the trees in protest before the government relented and replanted many elsewhere on the Tidal Basin. The memorial's circular, domed design deliberately echoed Jefferson's own home at Monticello and the Pantheon he admired.

The bronze statue at its centre was cast in plaster for the 1943 dedication because wartime metal restrictions made bronze unavailable; the actual bronze figure was not installed until 1947. Franklin Roosevelt, who championed the memorial, attended the dedication on Jefferson's two hundredth birthday.

Djenne sits on the floodplain of the Bani River, and that seasonal flooding is what made it valuable: goods could be moved by boat much of the year, and the city grew from around the 9th century into a market where gold and salt from further afield changed hands, alongside people sold into slavery along the same routes.

The city's mudbrick Great Mosque, rebuilt repeatedly on the same site since a first structure went up in the 13th century, is resurfaced with fresh mud by the community every year after the rainy season, a maintenance ritual that keeps a building this old still standing at all.

Long before the biblical trumpets, Jericho's inhabitants raised a stone wall over four metres high and a tower nearly nine metres tall beside a freshwater spring. Excavations by Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s dated this construction to roughly 8000 BCE, thousands of years before the settlement had any writing or pottery.
