Archaeologists still argue over what the wall was for. It could have kept out raiders drawn by the spring and stored grain, but its position also matches the path of flash floods off the nearby Judean hills, so some read it as flood defence that only later hardened into a fortification.

Daniel Libeskind's design has no obvious front door. Visitors enter through a neighbouring baroque building and descend into the zigzag structure through underground passages that cross at odd angles, one leading to a garden of tilted concrete columns, another dead-ending in a bare concrete tower called the Holocaust Void that is left unheated and largely unlit.

The building opened to the public in 2001, two years after construction finished, because it stood empty while curators decided what exhibition could match a structure that was already being read as a monument in its own right. Thin diagonal window slits, cut without a fixed pattern, are widely read as tracing lines between addresses once occupied by Berlin's Jewish community on a prewar map.

Chicago's John Hancock Center topped out in 1969 with a tapered black form and diagonal steel X-braces running up its exterior, a structural system engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan devised to let the tower resist wind without a bulky internal frame. The bracing let the tapered tower stack apartments, offices, parking and an observation deck in one building rather than several.

Khan's trussed-tube approach, first proven at scale here, cut the amount of steel needed compared with conventional skyscraper frames of the era and influenced tall buildings that followed it, including his own later Sears Tower. At 344 metres including its antennae, the Hancock was Chicago's second-tallest building at completion and remains one of the few towers where the structure's bracing is also its exterior decoration.

The Kowoj Maya settled around Lake Peten Itza in what is now northern Guatemala well after the great Classic Maya cities to the north had emptied out. Their lakeside towns belong to the Postclassic period, when Maya political life had shifted away from the monumental temple centres toward smaller, fortified settlements built for defence as much as ceremony.

Sites like Zacpeten sat on peninsulas jutting into the lake, an arrangement that limited access on the landward side and made the water itself part of the defences. Kowoj communities in this region survived, still practising traditional Maya religion, until Spanish forces finally conquered the last independent Maya kingdom there in 1697.

Ivan III hired Italian engineers, familiar with the fortifications of Milan, to rebuild Moscow's wooden citadel in brick between 1485 and 1495. Their triangular circuit of walls and 20 towers borrowed Italian military engineering while housing distinctly Russian cathedrals and palaces inside.

The walls were not always red: for a period under Catherine the Great they were whitewashed, and the deep red now associated with the Kremlin became fixed only after later restorations. Its towers acquired the ruby stars now on top only in the Soviet era, replacing the double-headed eagles that had marked imperial rule.

Los Angeles City Hall opened in 1928 at 452 feet, tall only because it was exempted from a 1904 municipal ordinance capping other buildings at 150 feet. That rule, meant to keep the city from crowding its streets with skyscrapers, effectively guaranteed City Hall's tower would dominate the skyline by law rather than by engineering ambition.

The height cap was repealed in 1957 once earthquake engineering and fire codes had advanced enough to make tall buildings safer, but City Hall was not actually overtaken until 1966, when the Union Bank building opened downtown. Its silhouette had already become a fixture of Los Angeles's image, appearing on the LAPD badge and in countless films before it lost its record.

Peter the Great ordered the canal in 1718 to give barges a way around Lake Ladoga, whose storms had wrecked hundreds of cargo vessels trying to reach the new capital at St Petersburg. Construction began in 1719 and the channel, linking the Neva and Volkhov rivers along the lake's southern shore, was finished in 1730, five years after Peter's death.

It was one of the largest hydraulic engineering projects attempted anywhere in Europe that century, dug largely by hand and forced labour over more than a decade. The canal kept goods bound for St Petersburg off the open lake entirely, and it stayed in active use until a second, deeper Ladoga canal was built alongside it in the 1860s.

Louisiana finished a second, parallel span of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in 1969, running alongside the original 1956 bridge to handle growing traffic between New Orleans and its northern suburbs. The new span was only about 15 metres longer than the first, but the pairing gave the crossing a combined length of nearly 38.4 kilometres, most of it with no land in sight in either direction.

Guinness World Records recognised the causeway as the longest bridge over continuous water on its completion, a title it held unchallenged for decades. China's Jiaozhou Bay Bridge opened in 2011 and Guinness split the category rather than hand over one title outright: Jiaozhou Bay took longest bridge over water overall, while the Louisiana causeway kept the record for the longest bridge over continuous water.

Almost all lapis lazuli used in the ancient Near East came from one place: the Sar-e-Sang mines in the Badakhshan mountains of what is now Afghanistan. Nowhere else was known to produce the deep blue stone in quantity, which made every piece found in an Egyptian or Mesopotamian tomb evidence of a very long supply chain.

Tutankhamun's burial mask uses lapis for the eyebrows and eyeliner around eyes rimmed with the stone, brought west over well over a thousand miles of mountain and desert. Sumerian cities such as Ur were trading it by the mid third millennium BCE, valuing it enough to bury it with their dead alongside gold.

Construction of Pisa's bell tower began in 1173 on ground too soft and uneven to support its weight evenly, and the tilt appeared before builders had even finished the third storey. Work then stopped for nearly a century because of wars, an accidental pause that let the unstable soil settle and probably kept the tower from toppling outright.

Engineers compensated for the lean by angling later storeys back toward vertical, giving the finished tower a slight banana curve rather than a straight slant. A twentieth century campaign of soil removal on the raised side reduced the tilt and stabilised the structure, work completed in 2001 after the tower had been closed to visitors for over a decade.

Ole Kirk Christiansen's small Danish carpentry firm had already been making wooden toys and plastic bricks for a decade when his son Godtfred filed the patent for the improved stud and tube coupling system in 1958. Earlier Lego bricks, and a similar British brick called Kiddicraft, could not grip each other securely enough to build tall or stable structures.

The new tube design let bricks clutch together firmly while still pulling apart by hand, and that geometry has stayed essentially unchanged since. A brick moulded in 1958 still fits one bought new today, a compatibility the company has protected through repeated patent and trademark disputes over the decades.

Lever Brothers built its Park Avenue headquarters as an advertisement for cleanliness itself. The tower's glass and steel skin, hung on a frame rather than walls that carried weight, could be washed by a mechanical rig running on tracks along its face, a novelty at the time meant to keep the soap company's own building visibly spotless.

Designed by Gordon Bunshaft at Skidmore, Owings and Merrill and finished in 1952, it raised its slab off the ground on stilts and left most of the site as open plaza, breaking from the solid masonry towers that had defined Park Avenue. Other architects copied the glass curtain wall for office towers across American cities through the following decade.

Thomas Edison did not invent the light bulb; incandescent lamps using platinum or carbon filaments had already been demonstrated by several inventors over the previous decades. What Edison's Menlo Park laboratory achieved in October 1879 was a carbonised filament, eventually cotton thread and later bamboo, that burned in a vacuum long enough and cheaply enough to be commercially viable.

Edison also built the surrounding system that made the bulb useful: generators, wiring, meters and sockets, patented and marketed together. His Pearl Street power station in lower Manhattan began supplying electric light to paying customers in 1882, turning the bulb from a laboratory curiosity into household infrastructure.

Ptolemy I began the lighthouse on the island of Pharos around 290 BCE, and it was finished under his son Ptolemy II close to 280 BCE. Ancient estimates put it above 100 metres tall, built in tapering stone stages, square base then octagonal then round, with a fire kept burning at the top and, according to later accounts, a mirror arrangement that could reflect sunlight far out to sea.

The lighthouse survived largely intact for well over a thousand years, longer than any of the other ancient Wonders, before a series of earthquakes between the tenth and fourteenth centuries brought it down in stages. Its remaining blocks were reused in the 1480s to build the fort that still occupies the site, Qaitbay Citadel, in modern Alexandria.

The memorial opened in May 1922 on reclaimed marshland along the Potomac, its site chosen only after decades of argument over whether a memorial to Lincoln should be a grand building at all or something plainer. Architect Henry Bacon modelled it on a Greek temple, with 36 columns representing the states of the Union at the time of Lincoln's death.

Sculptor Daniel Chester French's seated statue inside was carved from 28 blocks of Georgia marble, assembled so precisely that the joins are barely visible. The memorial's steps became a stage for civil rights history it was never designed for, most famously when Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'I Have a Dream' speech there in 1963.

The Lion Gate, built into Mycenae's citadel wall around 1250 BCE, is named for the relief above its lintel showing two lionesses flanking a central column, carved on a triangular limestone slab that lightens the load on the doorway beneath. It is the only large-scale sculpture known to survive from Mycenaean Greece.

The gate's lintel stone is estimated to weigh around twenty tonnes, set between jambs of similarly massive blocks. By the time classical Greeks visited the ruins centuries later, they no longer knew who had built it, which is part of why Cyclopean masonry, work credited to mythical giants, became the term for construction on this scale.

The Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in September 1830, built from the outset to run scheduled steam locomotives hauling both goods and paying passengers on double track between two major cities. Unlike the earlier Stockton and Darlington line, it never relied on horse traction for its passenger service, which is why historians usually credit it as the first true modern railway.

Its opening day was marred when the MP William Huskisson was struck and killed by Stephenson's Rocket while crossing the tracks to greet the Duke of Wellington, an early and widely reported demonstration of how fast the new locomotives actually moved. Despite the accident, the line proved so profitable that it set the template investors used to fund railways across Britain over the following decade.

Richard Rogers put the lifts, ductwork and staircases on the outside in steel and glass towers so the interior could stay open around a vast atrium, a decision that let the insurance market's trading floor keep its historic underwriting Room intact at the centre. Critics nicknamed it the inside-out building before most had set foot inside.

It became a Grade I listed building in 2011, the youngest structure ever given that protection in Britain, only twenty-five years after it opened. Listing normally follows decades of settled reputation, so Historic England's decision effectively fast-tracked a building whose services were, by design, meant to be replaced and repaired in view.

It was meant to be temporary. The wheel's five-year planning permission was tied to the millennium, and its designers, husband-and-wife architects David Marks and Julia Barfield, expected it to come down long before it became one of London's most photographed structures. It opened to the public on 9 March 2000, a few months late for the millennium itself, after the final capsules were fitted while the wheel was already turning.

At 135 metres it was the tallest observation wheel in the world when it opened, a title it held until the Star of Nanchang overtook it in 2006. Each of its 32 sealed glass capsules represents one of London's boroughs, and a full rotation takes about thirty minutes, slow enough that the wheel rarely stops to let passengers on.

The Metropolitan Railway opened in January 1863 between Paddington and Farringdon, built by the cut and cover method: dig a trench along the street, brick over it, then put the road back on top. Steam locomotives hauled the carriages, and smoke was meant to vent through gaps along the route, though passengers still complained about the choking air underground.

Around 38,000 people rode it on the opening day alone, showing there was real demand for a way to cross central London without fighting horse-drawn traffic on the surface. Electric traction did not arrive until the 1890s, decades after this first line proved the idea could work, and it remained smoky, steam-hauled and gas-lit for its first three decades.

President Francois Mitterrand chose I.M. Pei, a Chinese American architect with no previous major work in France, to redesign the entrance to a museum that traces its walls back to a twelfth century fortress. Parisians who objected to a glass pyramid beside a Renaissance palace called the scheme an act of vandalism before it was even built.

The structure is built from 673 glass panes rather than the often-repeated 666, a myth that stuck partly because of its satanic overtones. Beneath the glass, Pei's design solved a practical problem: it let daylight into a new subterranean lobby that could funnel far larger crowds into the museum's three wings than the old entrances ever could.

The resort's three curved towers lean outward at an angle steep enough that engineers built and tested a full-scale mockup of the connection before trusting the design, then linked the towers at the top with a single 340-metre platform holding the rooftop pool, longer than the Eiffel Tower laid on its side. It opened in stages through 2010, with the casino and hotel rooms operating months before the SkyPark and its pool were finished.

Architect Moshe Safdie designed the platform to read as a ship balanced across three hulls, a form chosen partly so the resort's silhouette would be identifiable from across the bay. The infinity pool sits 57 storeys up and became one of the most photographed swimming pools in the world within its first year open.

Architect Bertrand Goldberg designed Marina City to keep Chicagoans from fleeing to the suburbs, packing apartments, a theatre, a bowling alley, a marina and parking into two round concrete towers finished in 1964. The scalloped balconies gave each unit curved outdoor space instead of a flat ledge, and for a few years the towers were the tallest concrete structures and the tallest residential buildings in the world.

The lower third of each tower is an open-air parking ramp, the wedge-shaped floors visible from outside as the corn cob's husk. Goldberg had trained under Mies van der Rohe but rejected the glass box entirely, arguing that Chicago needed round forms and mixed uses rather than another rectangular slab, and the towers still function largely as he planned them, apartments above cars above a marina.

Thomas Telford's bridge across the Menai Strait opened on 30 January 1826 after seven years of work, carrying the Holyhead road from London toward the Irish ferry crossing. Its main span of 579 feet was the longest ever attempted for a bridge of any kind at the time, hung from wrought iron chains made of eyebars forged by William Hazledine.

The deck proved dangerously light and swayed alarmingly in strong winds, since Telford had no earlier suspension bridge of this scale to learn from, and it needed stiffening work in 1840 and again in 1893 to control the movement. It was the second bridge built to carry road traffic on suspension chains, after the smaller Union Bridge over the River Tweed in 1820.

Merdeka 118 topped out in Kuala Lumpur at 678.9 metres, reaching its full height in 2023 though its official opening followed in January 2024. Its 118 floors and tapering, faceted form were designed to echo the raised fist of Tunku Abdul Rahman as he declared Malaysian independence, or merdeka, in 1957, a moment the tower's name commemorates directly.

Only Dubai's Burj Khalifa stands higher, with Shanghai Tower third. The tower also overtook the nearby Petronas Towers as Malaysia's tallest structure, a title those towers had held since 1998, and its spire accounts for a large share of the headline height.

Bi Sheng's system in eleventh century China used individual characters formed from baked clay, cheap to make but fragile in use. Korea's Goryeo dynasty took the underlying idea, arranging reusable individual characters rather than carving a whole page as one woodblock, and recast it in bronze, a material sturdy enough for repeated printing runs.

A Korean text on Buddhist ritual is recorded as printed from metal type as early as 1234, decades before the Jikji of 1377, long cited as the oldest surviving book printed this way. Gutenberg's press, working from an unrelated tradition in Europe over two centuries later, is often credited as the first, but Korean printers had already solved the same problem.

Robert Peel, then home secretary, pushed the Metropolitan Police Act through Parliament in 1829, creating a uniformed force of about a thousand constables to patrol London outside the old City boundary. Officers were nicknamed bobbies and peelers after him, terms that have outlasted almost everything else about the original force.

Peel's instructions to the new force emphasised prevention over punishment and deliberately avoided military ranks and weapons, a contrast with the armed gendarmeries already operating on the continent. The model spread to other British cities within a decade and was copied, with local variation, across much of the English-speaking world.

The Millau Viaduct carries a motorway across the Tarn river valley in southern France on seven slender concrete pylons, the tallest of which rises 343 metres including its mast, taller than the Eiffel Tower. Engineer Michel Virlogeux worked with architect Norman Foster on a cable-stayed design light enough to be pushed out from both ends of the gorge and joined in the middle rather than built up from the valley floor.

It opened on 16 December 2004, finishing three years of construction that had to account for wind gusts strong enough to close the valley's older roads. At a structural height of 336.4 metres it became the tallest bridge in the world, a record it still holds, though the far longer Danyang-Kunshan viaduct in China overtook it in overall length within a few years.

The dome on the Greenwich peninsula was built on reclaimed, contaminated gasworks land as the centrepiece of Britain's millennium celebrations, its fabric roof suspended from twelve steel masts meant to evoke the twelve months of the year. It opened its exhibition to the public on 1 January 2000 after Queen Elizabeth II and Tony Blair marked the new year inside on the previous night.

Visitor numbers fell well short of the twelve million projected, and the exhibition closed at a loss that became a byword for costly public projects gone wrong. The structure itself survived: renamed the O2 Arena in 2007, it reopened as one of London's busiest concert venues, proving the building outlasted the millennium show it was built for.

Cahokia grew rapidly around 1050 on the floodplain across the Mississippi from what is now St Louis, and at its height held somewhere between 10,000 and 20,000 people spread across more than a hundred earthen mounds. That made it the largest settlement north of Mexico before European contact, comparable in size to contemporary London.

Monks Mound, its largest earthwork, covers about five hectares at the base and was built up in stages using only baskets and human labour, no draft animals or wheeled carts. By around 1350 the site had been largely abandoned, for reasons still debated among archaeologists, including drought, resource strain and political upheaval.

The Moche built along Peru's northern coast without writing or a currency, ruling through irrigation-fed valleys rather than a single capital. Their platform mounds, made of millions of sun-dried adobe bricks, were topped with painted temples where elite burials and ritual sacrifice took place, known largely from grave goods and painted pottery scenes.

Huaca del Sol, the largest of these structures, once stood over 40 metres high before a colonial-era river diversion and looting stripped away much of its bulk. What survives is still one of the largest adobe structures ever built in the Americas, and excavation there continues to reveal how the mound grew in stages over centuries.

Mohenjo-daro, built along the Indus in present-day Pakistan around 2500 BCE, laid its streets on a grid and ran covered brick drains beneath most houses, a sanitation system many cities would not match for thousands of years. Its Great Bath, a watertight brick tank sunk into a raised platform, suggests a shared civic or ritual use rather than private plumbing alone.

Excavated from the 1920s, the city has produced no palace, temple or evidence of a single ruler, an absence that has left its social structure disputed. It was abandoned by around 1900 BCE, and its script, found on small stamped seals, has never been deciphered, so the city's own name for itself is unknown.

The mounds were not tombs alone. Mississippian communities, emerging from around 800 CE across the southeastern and midwestern United States, built flat-topped earthen platforms to raise temples, chiefs' houses and civic space above the surrounding land, moving the earth basket by basket rather than with any beast of burden.

Cahokia, near modern St Louis, grew into the largest of these settlements, its central Monks Mound covering roughly six hectares at the base and rising about 30 metres, built up in stages over generations by a population that, at its peak, likely rivalled contemporary European cities.

Sculptor Gutzon Borglum died in March 1941 with the memorial still unfinished, and his son Lincoln took over the final months of work. Funding ran out that October, so the carving stopped rather than reaching the completion Borglum had planned; the four heads were declared finished as they stood, without the torsos originally envisioned.

Dynamite did most of the rough work. Crews blasted away roughly 90 percent of the granite before finer tools shaped the faces, and no workers died during the fourteen years of carving, an unusual record for a project of that scale and period.

The Mouseion of Alexandria was founded around 290 BCE under Ptolemy I, not as a museum in the modern sense but as a research institution dedicated to the Muses, housing scholars on royal stipends alongside the library that became attached to it. Its members included Euclid, whose geometry textbook remained in use for over two thousand years, and later Eratosthenes, who calculated the earth's circumference there.

The library it held is usually remembered for burning, but its decline was gradual, worn down by funding cuts, political upheaval, and repeated damage over centuries rather than by any single fire. The institution itself outlasted the library, continuing to support scholars in Alexandria for centuries after the Ptolemaic dynasty ended.

Mycenaean builders around 1400 BCE walled their hilltop citadels, Mycenae and Tiryns among them, with limestone blocks so large that later Greeks, unable to explain how they were moved, credited the work to the Cyclopes. Modern archaeologists still call this method Cyclopean masonry, even though it was ordinary human labour with ramps and levers.

Tiryns went further underground, with a corbelled gallery built into its own walls, while Mycenae's citadel controlled the routes through the Argolid plain. These fortifications outlasted the palace bureaucracies inside them: when Mycenaean civilisation collapsed around 1200 BCE, the walls themselves stood for centuries after the halls behind them had emptied.

Petra sits in a narrow sandstone gorge in southern Jordan, reachable only through a slot canyon called the Siq. The Nabataeans, an Arab trading people who controlled routes carrying frankincense and spices between Arabia and the Mediterranean, made it their capital, and the facades cut into the rock face, including the Treasury, were carved rather than built up from the ground.

The city's wealth came from tolls on caravans rather than farming, which is unusual for a capital in such dry terrain; cisterns and channels cut into the rock captured seasonal flash floods to keep the population supplied with water. Rome annexed the Nabataean kingdom in 106 CE, after which Petra's importance as a trade hub gradually declined.

Emperor Shomu ordered Todai-ji built to house a bronze Buddha statue roughly 15 metres tall, a project so demanding it reportedly used most of Japan's available bronze and nearly bankrupted the treasury. The temple's main hall, the Daibutsuden, was completed in 752 and became the centrepiece of a network of provincial temples meant to protect the state through Buddhist ritual.

Fire destroyed the original hall twice, and the building standing today dates from a 1709 rebuild that is noticeably smaller than what Shomu raised, roughly two thirds the length of the original. Even reduced, it remains the largest wooden building in the world.

The Nazca desert receives almost no rainfall, so their engineers dug puquios, underground galleries reaching down 10 to 15 metres to tap the water table and channel it toward fields and settlements. Spiral entrances, called ojos or eyes, gave workers access for maintenance and let wind push air down into the tunnels to keep water moving.

Building them required knowing exactly where the water table sat across a wide area without modern surveying instruments, a task the Nazca solved through generations of trial and adjustment. More than thirty of the puquios are still functioning today, supplying water to farms in the same valleys nearly two thousand years after they were first cut.

An English fleet under Richard Nicolls sailed into New Amsterdam's harbour in 1664 and demanded the Dutch colony's surrender. Governor Peter Stuyvesant wanted to resist, but the settlers, outnumbered and unsupported by the Dutch West India Company, pressed him to give up the town without a shot being fired.

Nicolls renamed it New York after James, Duke of York, the king's brother who held the colony's proprietary rights. The Dutch briefly recaptured it in 1673 during a later war, calling it New Orange, but ceded it back to England for good the following year under the Treaty of Westminster.

Newgrange, in Ireland's Boyne Valley, was raised around 3200 BCE from an estimated two hundred thousand tonnes of stone, its facade faced in white quartz brought from Wicklow, some 70 kilometres away, with no wheeled transport available to move it. The mound covers a passage tomb whose narrow chamber leads to a corbelled roof that has kept the interior dry for over five thousand years.

A precisely aligned roof box above the entrance lets sunlight reach the inner chamber only around the winter solstice, a feature rediscovered by archaeologists in 1967 rather than known continuously since. It predates Stonehenge and the Great Pyramid of Giza by several centuries, built by people who left no writing to explain why.

Le Corbusier had spent decades as the leading voice of stark, machine age modernism, so the curved concrete chapel he built on a hilltop at Ronchamp in eastern France surprised even his admirers. It replaced an earlier church destroyed by shelling during the Second World War, and its client was the Catholic Church rather than any secular commission.

Thick walls curve and lean, punctured by small irregular windows of coloured glass, and a heavy roof appears to float above them without visible support. Critics who expected another glass box accused him of abandoning rationalism; Le Corbusier himself described the design as answering the site's particular light rather than any doctrine.

In February 1825 the Ohio legislature authorized two canals at once, the Ohio and Erie running roughly from Cleveland to Portsmouth, and the Miami and Erie linking Cincinnati toward Toledo, betting the young state's finances on giving its farmers a water route to markets on both the Great Lakes and the Ohio River.

Construction relied heavily on Irish and German immigrant labourers digging by hand through swamp and forest, and outbreaks of malaria and cholera killed workers along the routes. The canals took years to finish, but they cut the cost of moving grain and produce so sharply that towns along their banks, including Akron and Dayton, grew rapidly once the water started flowing.

Six wells had already come up dry or uneconomic before the seventh, Dammam Well No. 7, struck oil in commercial quantities on 3 March 1938. American geologists working for Standard Oil of California had spent years testing the Arabian coast on a concession first signed in 1933, and the company's patience with a well nicknamed Prosperity Well was near its end.

The find turned a subsistence economy built on pearling and pilgrimage revenue into one of the largest oil producers on earth within a generation. Aramco, the company that grew out of that concession, later became fully Saudi owned; the kingdom holds some of the largest proven reserves of any nation.

One World Trade Center opened in November 2014 on the northwest corner of the original World Trade Center site, replacing the north tower destroyed in 2001. Its roof reaches 417 metres, matching the height of the old twin towers, but a broadcast spire brings its official tip to a symbolic 1,776 feet.

No taller building stands anywhere in the Americas, though Asia and the Middle East had already passed it well before it opened. Construction took nearly a decade after the site was cleared, delayed by disputes over financing, security requirements, and who would occupy the tower once it was finished.

The crossing between Denmark and Sweden is not one continuous bridge. Cars and trains cross a cable-stayed bridge for about 8 kilometres, then drop onto an artificial island, Peberholm, before diving into a submerged tunnel for the final stretch under the shipping lanes into Copenhagen. The tunnel section exists because Denmark's military and aviation authorities would not allow a structure tall enough to be a hazard so close to the airport.

It opened to traffic on 1 July 2000 after Queen Margrethe II and King Carl XVI Gustaf jointly inaugurated it, and it remains the longest combined road and rail bridge in Europe. Peberholm, built entirely from spoil dredged for the tunnel, was left unlandscaped and has since become an unplanned nature reserve.

The palace at Knossos, on Crete, was rebuilt several times after earthquake damage, and the layout visible to visitors today dates mostly from a rebuilding around 1700 BCE. Its maze of interconnected rooms and storerooms, without an obvious single throughway, likely fed the later Greek legend of the labyrinth built to hold the Minotaur.

British archaeologist Arthur Evans excavated the site from 1900 and reconstructed sections in concrete, repainting frescoes based on fragmentary evidence, a restoration since criticised for showing more of his own guesswork than the Bronze Age original. The palace was finally destroyed by fire around 1350 BCE, ending Knossos as the Minoans' main centre.

Pakal the Great ruled Palenque for 68 years, from 615 to 683, one of the longest reigns recorded anywhere in the ancient world, and the city's major building programme, including the Temple of Inscriptions, belongs to that reign and the decades right after it under his son.

Pakal's tomb, sealed inside the temple's pyramid, was not opened until 1952, when archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier found his skeleton beneath a carved sarcophagus lid weighing about five tonnes, jade mask still in place, one of the few undisturbed royal Maya burials ever recovered.

Most Indian temples of this era were carved from a single rock outcrop, the way Ellora's were. The Shore Temple at Mahabalipuram, raised under the Pallava king Narasimhavarman II around 700, was instead built up from cut granite blocks, one of the earliest structural stone temples to survive in southern India rather than a rock-cut one.

Set directly on the Bay of Bengal shoreline, it has taken centuries of salt spray and monsoon erosion that inland temples never faced, and a 2004 tsunami briefly exposed underwater stone formations offshore that some archaeologists read as remains of other, now-submerged shore structures.

The island's palm shape was built entirely from dredged sand, pumped from the Gulf floor and shaped by a positioning system rather than by any land survey, since there was no land there to survey before construction began in 2001. A breakwater crescent, made largely from quarried rock, was placed around the fronds to hold the sand in place against the sea.

Land reclamation was substantially finished by 2006, though villas and apartment towers along the fronds continued to be built and sold for years afterward. It was the first and largest of three planned palm-shaped islands off Dubai's coast, and it remains visible from orbit, a fact its developers publicised heavily at the time.

The canal opened to shipping in August 1914, a decade after the United States took over a project that had already ruined a French company under Ferdinand de Lesseps, whose earlier attempt collapsed amid disease and cost overruns in the 1880s. American engineers switched from a sea-level design to a system of locks that raise ships over the isthmus using an artificial lake.

Malaria and yellow fever killed thousands of workers before doctor William Gorgas organised a campaign against mosquito breeding grounds that made the site survivable for the workforce that followed. Panama did not gain full control of the canal until a 1999 handover under treaties signed two decades earlier.

Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon around 126 on the site of an earlier temple that had burned down, but he kept the original founder's name, Marcus Agrippa, carved over the entrance rather than his own. The dome spans 43.4 metres and the building's height matches that span exactly, so a sphere would fit inside it perfectly.

Builders thinned the concrete toward the top and used progressively lighter aggregate, pumice near the crown, to keep the mass manageable without steel reinforcement. It remained the world's largest dome until Florence Cathedral's was finished in the 1400s, but among unreinforced concrete domes specifically it has never been surpassed.

Athens finished the Parthenon's main structure in 438 BCE, though decorative carving on its friezes continued for several more years, funded partly by tribute Athens collected from other Greek city-states through the Delian League. Built to replace an earlier, unfinished temple destroyed by the Persians, it held a giant gold and ivory statue of Athena by the sculptor Phidias.

The building later became a Byzantine church, then a mosque under Ottoman rule, and survived largely intact until 1687, when Venetian forces besieging the Ottoman garrison fired on gunpowder stored inside, blowing out much of its centre. Many of its remaining sculptures were removed to Britain by Lord Elgin in the early nineteenth century and remain in London.

Ground broke on 11 September 1941, three months before Pearl Harbor, on a site the War Department chose partly because its odd boundaries forced the building into five sides rather than the square originally intended. Roosevelt disliked the shape and asked for a redesign, but the change came too late to alter the plan without losing time the war effort could not spare.

Workers finished the building in sixteen months, working around the clock in shifts, using ramps instead of many of the elevators to save steel for the war. At the time it opened in January 1943 it held the title of largest office building by floor area; later buildings elsewhere have since surpassed that figure.

Darius the Great began Persepolis around 518 BCE on a stone terrace in the hills of southern Iran, not as a capital for daily administration but as a ceremonial seat for royal audiences and the Persian New Year festival, Nowruz. Its Apadana hall, ringed with columns over twenty metres tall, could reportedly hold thousands of guests at once.

Construction stretched across several reigns, with Xerxes and later kings adding buildings over roughly a century. Alexander the Great's army burned Persepolis in 330 BCE, an act ancient sources describe as deliberate and possibly drunken, and the fire's traces are still visible in the site's blackened stone today.

Cesar Pelli designed the towers' floor plan around an eight-pointed star drawn from Islamic geometric patterns, a nod to Malaysia's Muslim majority worked into a building otherwise defined by steel and glass. The two towers were built by separate contractors racing each other, one Japanese and one South Korean, and are linked by a double-decker skybridge at the 41st and 42nd floors.

They held the title of world's tallest building from 1998 until 2004, when Taipei 101 overtook them, ending a run during which Petronas had beaten Chicago's Sears Tower on a technicality: architectural spires counted toward height, antennas did not. They remain the tallest twin towers ever built, a narrower record nothing since has bothered to contest.

Architects Richard Rogers and Renzo Piano won the competition for Paris's new cultural centre with an idea that shocked the jury: put the building's structure, escalators and service pipes on the outside, painted in bright primary colours, so every floor inside stayed open and uninterrupted. It opened in 1977 as the Centre Pompidou, named for the president who had commissioned it.

Parisians nicknamed it the refinery, and much of the initial press was hostile to a building that looked, deliberately, like its own plumbing turned inside out. The colour coding was functional rather than decorative: blue ducts carry air, green pipes carry water, yellow housing covers electrical lines, and red marks the escalators and lifts that carry visitors up the building's exterior.

Darius I organised the Angareion along the Royal Road, a route of roughly 2,500 kilometres linking Sardis in Lydia to Susa in Persia. Post houses stood at set intervals, each keeping fresh horses and a rested rider ready, so a message could be handed off rather than carried the whole distance by one exhausted courier.

Herodotus described the system admiringly, writing that neither snow, rain, heat nor darkness stopped the couriers from finishing their route, a line later echoed on the facade of the New York City Post Office. Royal messages that would take an army three months on foot reportedly crossed the same distance in about a week using the relay.

The fifth Dalai Lama began the Potala Palace in 1645 on a hill in Lhasa already associated with an earlier fortress, building it as both the seat of Tibetan government and his personal residence once he had unified religious and political authority over Tibet. The White Palace, for administration, and the later Red Palace, for religious functions, were built in separate phases.

The Dalai Lama's death partway through construction was kept secret for years so the building could continue uninterrupted, a concealment managed by his regent, Desi Sangye Gyatso. The finished palace rises over 100 metres up the hillside across thirteen storeys, and it now houses the tombs of several past Dalai Lamas.

Prambanan went up in central Java in the mid 9th century, not long after the Buddhist Borobudur nearby, and its scale reads as a statement: a Hindu dynasty answering a Buddhist monument with one of its own, dedicated to the Trimurti of Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva.

Its central Shiva shrine rises about 47 metres, taller than any single structure at Borobudur, over a complex of originally more than 200 smaller shrines. Earthquakes toppled much of it over the centuries, and restoration using original stones has continued into the 21st century.

Pueblo Bonito was not built in one campaign. Ancestral Puebloan builders raised it in phases from around 860 to 1130, and its final D-shaped footprint held over 350 ground-floor rooms, some estimates running past 600 once its upper storeys are counted, rising four floors on the north side.

The great house held 32 kivas and three great kivas, circular rooms used for gatherings and ceremony, but shows little evidence of everyday domestic life: few hearths, little household refuse. Archaeologists now read it less as a crowded residence and more as a ceremonial and administrative centre for a much wider Chacoan world.

Egyptian records from the Old Kingdom describe expeditions to a land called Punt, sending back gold, myrrh, incense, ebony and live animals including baboons. The earliest such voyage is credited to the reign of Sahure around 2500 BCE, reached by ship down the Red Sea rather than overland, since no land route between Egypt and Punt is attested.

Punt's exact location was never recorded and remains debated among scholars, with proposals ranging along the coasts of modern Eritrea, Sudan and Somalia. The relationship endured for well over a thousand years, most famously in reliefs at Hatshepsut's temple at Deir el-Bahari showing Puntite houses built on stilts.

Khufu's pyramid at Giza rose to about 146 metres around 2560 BCE and held the record as the tallest structure ever built by people for roughly 3,800 years, a span not broken until England's Lincoln Cathedral added a spire in the thirteenth century. No blueprints or worker rosters explaining the exact building method have survived, only later, often contradictory, Greek and Egyptian accounts.

Papyri found at the Red Sea port of Wadi al-Jarf, logged by an official named Merer, describe boat crews hauling limestone up the Nile to the site, the closest thing to a contemporary construction record that exists. The pyramid is also the only one of the ancient world's Seven Wonders still substantially standing.

Radio City Music Hall opened in December 1932 as the centrepiece of the new Rockefeller Center, built during the Depression's depths as a gamble that New Yorkers would still pay for spectacle. Its original booking policy, live variety stage shows before each film, flopped within weeks and the venue quickly switched to the movie-and-stage-show format that made it famous.

Designer Donald Deskey's Art Deco interior, all sweeping curves, gold leaf and indirect lighting, was considered radical for a theatre of its size, seating close to 6,000 people beneath a fan-shaped ceiling meant to evoke a sunset. The Rockettes, the resident dance troupe, had already been performing elsewhere in the city for several years before the hall gave them a permanent stage.

Venice's earlier crossings at this point on the Grand Canal were wooden and had collapsed or burned more than once, so the city held a competition for a permanent stone replacement, choosing Antonio da Ponte's design over proposals from Michelangelo and Palladio among others. The single-span bridge, with shops built into rows along its top, was completed in 1591.

Engineers of the time doubted a stone arch that flat could hold its own weight over such a wide span, and da Ponte's foundations, driven deep into the canal's mud on more than 6,000 wooden piles, proved them wrong. It remained the only bridge crossing the Grand Canal until the nineteenth century.

John D. Rockefeller Jr. had originally leased the land to build a new home for the Metropolitan Opera. The opera pulled out after the 1929 crash, leaving him committed to a 24 year lease on land he no longer had a tenant for, so his own company built an entire commercial complex instead to cover the payments.

Fourteen Art Deco buildings went up between 1932 and 1939, employing tens of thousands of workers during the Depression's worst years. Diego Rivera's mural for the lobby of the flagship tower was destroyed unfinished after he refused to remove a portrait of Lenin, and was replaced by a different artist's work.

Appius Claudius Caecus, serving as censor, began the Via Appia in 312 BCE to move troops and supplies south during Rome's wars with the Samnites. It ran from Rome to Capua and was later extended to the port of Brindisi, giving it the nickname regina viarum, queen of roads.

Its surface set the pattern the rest of the network would follow: layers of gravel and sand under fitted stone paving, cambered to drain rainwater to the sides. Sections of the original paving still exist south of Rome, and the road remained a working route for centuries after Appius Claudius laid its first stretch.

By around 200, the Roman road network had grown from military supply lines into a system spanning over 400,000 kilometres, of which roughly 80,000 were paved with stone. Roads were built in layers, with a cambered stone surface over compacted gravel and sand, designed to drain and to last under legions and wheeled traffic alike.

Distances were marked with milestones counted from a golden marker in the Forum, which gave rise to the phrase all roads lead to Rome. Many routes across Europe and North Africa still follow the Roman alignment today, not because the stone survived but because the same valleys and passes remained the easiest way through.

Romanesque takes its name from a nineteenth century comparison: its round arches and thick masonry walls echoed Roman construction, even though the style itself grew up across Western Europe centuries after Rome fell. Builders working with limited engineering knowledge relied on sheer mass, piling stone thick enough to carry a heavy vaulted roof without collapsing.

That reliance on mass kept windows small and interiors dim, which church builders offset with decorative arcading, carved capitals and bands of blind arches running along exterior walls. The style dominated European church building through the eleventh and much of the twelfth century, until pointed arches and ribbed vaulting let Gothic architecture carry the same loads with far less wall.

Roman tradition, fixed by the scholar Varro, dated the city's founding to 753 BCE, when Romulus supposedly killed his twin brother Remus in a dispute over which hill to build on and named the settlement after himself. There is no contemporary record from that year; the date was worked out centuries later by counting back through lists of kings and consuls.

Archaeology on the Palatine Hill has found huts and postholes from around the same period, evidence of real settlement there even if the twins and the she-wolf who supposedly raised them are legend. Romans kept using this founding date as an era, ab urbe condita, for counting years throughout their history.

In September 2021 the Tower of the Virgin Mary, the second tallest of Sagrada Familia's towers, was topped out with a twelve-pointed star. It was a step towards the taller central Tower of Jesus Christ, still under construction, which is designed to reach 172.5 metres and make the basilica the tallest church building in the world.

Antoni Gaudi took over the project in 1883 and worked on it until his death in 1926, by which point less than a quarter of the structure existed. Construction has continued since on donations and ticket revenue alone, without state or church funding, more than a century after he died having seen barely one tower finished.

Alexander the Great knew the city as Maracanda when he captured it in 329 BCE, but archaeology places settlement in the Zeravshan valley centuries earlier, around the eighth or seventh century BCE. Its position between the Tien Shan mountains and the Central Asian steppe made it a natural stop for anyone moving goods between China, India and Persia.

The city changed hands repeatedly, held in turn by Persians, Greeks, Turkic and Arab conquerors, and later Mongols under Genghis Khan, who razed much of it in 1220. It was rebuilt again under Timur in the fourteenth century as his capital, and people have lived there without a break through every one of those destructions.

Schonbrunn began as a hunting lodge the Habsburgs rebuilt after the Ottomans besieged Vienna in 1683, and the original design by Johann Bernhard Fischer von Erlach was scaled back for cost before Empress Maria Theresa had it reworked into the pale yellow palace seen today. The main building work finished around 1749, though decoration of its interiors continued for years afterward.

Maria Theresa used the palace as her main summer residence and raised sixteen children partly within its walls, including the future Marie Antoinette. A six year old Mozart is said to have performed for the empress there in 1762, and the palace's grounds later held one of the world's oldest continuously operating zoos, founded in 1752.

Phyllis Lambert, the daughter of Seagram's president, talked her father out of a conventional design and pushed the commission toward Mies van der Rohe instead, against the advice of company executives who wanted something safer. The bronze toned tower that resulted, finished in 1958, cost far more per square foot than any office building built up to that point.

Mies set the tower back from Park Avenue behind an open plaza, a break from the street wall other buildings kept, and used non structural bronze coloured I beams on the facade purely for their visual rhythm. The plaza and setback became the model city zoning later rewarded, copied by towers across Manhattan that offered public space for extra height.

Sears Tower topped out in Chicago in 1973 using a bundled tube design, nine square tubes of varying heights fused together, that let engineer Fazlur Rahman Khan build taller without a proportionally heavier structure. At 442 metres it overtook the World Trade Center's towers in New York to become the world's tallest building, a title it held for nearly 25 years.

Malaysia's Petronas Towers overtook it in 1998, aided by a measurement dispute over whether decorative spires counted toward height, and Chicago lost the world record it had first claimed with the Home Insurance Building in 1885. Sears itself moved out of the building years before the company's decline, and it was renamed the Willis Tower in 2009 after an insurance broker took over the naming rights.

Seattle built the Space Needle for the 1962 Century 21 Exposition, a world's fair built around the coming space age five years after Sputnik. At 184 metres it was the tallest structure west of the Mississippi when it opened, with a rotating restaurant near the top and an observation deck that drew millions of fair visitors over six months.

Engineers designed the tower's tripod base to survive winds of 320 kilometres an hour and earthquakes far stronger than any recorded in the region, since nobody wanted a landmark that toppled on live television. The fair itself closed at a profit, an unusual outcome for a world's fair, and the Needle outlasted every other structure built for the event to become the city's most recognisable image.

The Seikan Tunnel runs beneath the Tsugaru Strait linking Honshu and Hokkaido, with about 23 kilometres of its 53.85 kilometre length actually under the seabed, deeper below sea level than any tunnel built before it. Construction took roughly twenty-four years, driven partly by a 1954 ferry disaster that killed over a thousand people crossing the same strait in a typhoon.

It remained the world's longest rail tunnel until Switzerland's Gotthard Base Tunnel opened in 2016, though Seikan still carries a longer undersea section than the Channel Tunnel that opened six years after it. Bullet trains only began running through it in 2016, decades after the tunnel itself was finished, once the track gauge was converted for high-speed use.

Renzo Piano's tower tapers to an open, unfinished-looking spire rather than a flat roof or dome, a shape he sketched, according to his own account, on the back of a menu while discussing the site with the developer. Construction reached its full height of 310 metres in 2012, though fitting out the offices, apartments and hotel inside continued into the following year before all of them opened to occupants.

It became the tallest building in the United Kingdom and in Western Europe, overtaking Frankfurt's Commerzbank Tower, a record it still holds. Its glass panels were designed to reflect the sky rather than a fixed colour, so the tower's appearance from the ground changes constantly with the weather over London.

Japan opened the Tokaido Shinkansen on 1 October 1964, nine days before the Tokyo Olympics began, running trains between Tokyo and Osaka at up to 210 kilometres an hour. It was built on entirely new, dedicated track rather than shared rail, which is what let it run that fast: existing lines elsewhere were too curved and too crowded with slower traffic to be pushed past roughly half that speed.

The line's rounded, bullet-shaped nose gave the trains their English nickname, though in Japan they are simply Shinkansen, new trunk line. In six decades of operation the network has recorded no passenger fatalities from a derailment or collision, a safety record built on dedicated track, automatic braking and staff drilled to stop trains within seconds of any earthquake warning.

The pagoda went up in Bagan after Anawrahta's conquest of the Mon kingdom of Thaton, a campaign traditionally dated to 1057 that gave him control of Thaton's religious texts and, according to Burmese chronicles, relics that included strands of hair from the Buddha.

The pagoda's name means golden hair relic, referring to that tradition. Built as a bell-shaped stupa rather than the temple style Bagan later became known for, it was among the earliest major religious monuments in a city that held thousands of temples and pagodas across the plain by the thirteenth century.

By around 100, the overland routes linking Han China to the Roman Mediterranean were carrying goods through a chain of middlemen rather than any single trader making the whole journey. Silk moved west through Central Asian oases such as Kashgar and Samarkand, while glassware, wool and silver moved east, changing hands at every stop.

No merchant crossed the full distance; Roman writers knew silk came from the east without knowing much about China itself, and vice versa. The name Silk Road was coined by a nineteenth century German geographer, not by anyone who used the routes, but the exchange it describes had already reshaped diets, religions and metalwork across Eurasia by this period.

The Flyer opened in 2008 at 165 metres tall, overtaking the Star of Nanchang to become the tallest observation wheel in the world, a title measured by overall height rather than diameter since the wheel itself sits on a raised terminal building rather than the ground. Its 28 air-conditioned capsules were built large enough to hold twenty-eight passengers each, closer to a small room than a typical Ferris wheel cabin.

It kept the height record for about six years until the High Roller opened in Las Vegas in 2014 at 167.6 metres, and Dubai's taller Ain Dubai has since overtaken both. The Flyer briefly closed in 2008 after an electrical fire stopped it mid-rotation, stranding passengers for hours before they were winched down.

Stamford Raffles landed on the island in January 1819 looking for a base to counter Dutch control of the region's shipping lanes, and found a small fishing settlement of a few hundred people under a local Malay chief. He negotiated a treaty with the Sultan of Johor and the island's Temenggong that let the East India Company set up a trading post there.

Raffles left within days, handing running of the settlement to William Farquhar, and returned only a few times afterward, yet Singapore grew fast under free trade rules that waived the duties charged at Dutch ports nearby. Within a few decades it had become one of the busiest ports on the route between India and China.

Pope Sixtus IV had the chapel built as the pope's private chapel within the Vatican, finishing it in 1481 with its walls painted by artists including Perugino and Botticelli. Michelangelo's ceiling, the image most people picture, came almost three decades later, painted between 1508 and 1512 at the order of a different pope, Julius II.

Michelangelo returned in the 1530s to paint the Last Judgment on the altar wall, work that provoked complaints over nudity and led to loincloths being added to several figures after his death. The chapel still serves its original administrative purpose: cardinals gather there to elect each new pope.

A storm in 1850 stripped the turf off a sand dune on Orkney's Bay of Skaill and exposed stone houses that had lain buried for millennia. Skara Brae's Neolithic residents built with slabs of local flagstone rather than wood, which is scarce on the islands, and that choice is why beds, dressers and storage boxes survived instead of rotting away.

The village was occupied for roughly six centuries before being abandoned around 2500 BCE, its houses connected by covered passages that let people move between them without going outside into Orkney's wind. Because stone furniture lasted where timber elsewhere did not, Skara Brae shows domestic Neolithic life in more detail than almost any comparable site in Europe.

The Hebrew Bible credits Solomon with completing Jerusalem's First Temple after seven years of construction, using cedar shipped from Lebanon and skilled masons supplied by Hiram, king of Tyre. No archaeological remains of the building itself have been confirmed, since the site, the Temple Mount, remains too sensitive to excavate freely.

The building housed the Ark of the Covenant in an inner chamber, the Holy of Holies, entered only by the high priest and only once a year. It stood for roughly three and a half centuries until Babylonian forces under Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed it in 586 BCE, an event that reshaped Jewish religious life around exile and later return.

Song Dynasty shipwrights built vessels with watertight bulkheads dividing the hull into separate sealed compartments, so a hole in one section would not sink the whole ship, an innovation that took European shipbuilding centuries to adopt. Their junks also carried multiple masts and stern-mounted rudders, letting them sail further from the coast than earlier Chinese ships had managed.

Chinese navigators were among the first to use a magnetic compass at sea, described in a Song text from the early twelfth century, letting ships hold a course out of sight of land. Combined with government-licensed ports and paper trade documents, this let Song merchants reach as far as the Persian Gulf and East Africa by the early 1100s.

The Great Sphinx was carved from a single outcrop of bedrock left over after quarrying stone for the pyramids nearby, rather than assembled from blocks. Most Egyptologists date it to the reign of Khafre, around 2500 BCE, and read its face as a portrait of that pharaoh, though no inscription from the time names its builder or purpose.

Sand buried the statue up to its shoulders for long stretches of its history, and it was cleared repeatedly by different rulers, including an account of Thutmose IV excavating it in the fifteenth century BCE after, he claimed, the Sphinx spoke to him in a dream. The nose, often blamed on Napoleon's soldiers, was already missing before he arrived in Egypt.

Switzerland opened the St Gotthard Road Tunnel in September 1980 after roughly a decade of boring through the Alps between Goschenen and Airolo, giving drivers a route under the mountains that had previously demanded a long, snowbound pass or a rail car-shuttle. At almost 17 kilometres it became the longest road tunnel in the world on opening.

The record did not last two decades: Norway's Laerdal Tunnel overtook it in 2000, and several tunnels in Asia have since pushed the Gotthard further down the list. The tunnel is a single bore carrying traffic in both directions, a design that has made it prone to serious fires from head-on collisions, including one in 2001 that killed eleven people and shut the route for months.

Wren's dome was declared finished in 1708, thirty five years after work began, and by one account the last stone was laid by his son under his own supervision. Parliament had docked part of Wren's salary years earlier for slow progress, so he was working under a financial penalty even as he finished one of the largest cathedrals in Europe.

The dome itself was a structural gamble: an outer timber shell for the skyline view, an inner brick cone carrying the actual weight, and a hidden brick dome between the two holding it all together. It replaced the medieval St Paul's, which had burned in the Great Fire of London in 1666 and was already in poor repair before that.

Pope Julius II ordered the old fourth century basilica torn down and a new one begun in 1506, appointing Donato Bramante as architect for a design centred on a vast dome over the traditional site of Saint Peter's grave. Selling indulgences to help fund the project became one of the grievances Martin Luther listed eleven years later when he broke with Rome.

Building continued for well over a century under a succession of architects including Michelangelo, who redesigned the dome, and it was not consecrated until 1626. The finished basilica held the title of the world's largest church for centuries afterward.

The statue was dedicated on 28 October 1886, a gift from France meant to mark a century of American independence, though it arrived ten years late because both countries struggled to fund their halves of the project. Frenchman Joseph Pulitzer used his newspaper to raise the final money for the pedestal from ordinary readers after wealthier donors balked at the cost.

Sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi built the copper skin over an iron framework designed by Gustave Eiffel, whose lattice tower would rise in Paris three years later. The torch has been closed to the public since a 1916 explosion at a nearby munitions depot damaged the arm, and visitors have not been allowed up it since.

The Statue of Unity was unveiled on 31 October 2018 on Sadhu Bet island in Gujarat, on what would have been Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel's birthday. Patel was India's first deputy prime minister and the figure credited with persuading hundreds of princely states to join the Indian union after independence, the unity the statue's name refers to.

At 182 metres it passed China's Spring Temple Buddha to become the tallest statue in the world, nearly twice the height of the Statue of Liberty including its pedestal. It took about three years to build and reportedly cost over four hundred million dollars, funded partly by melting down farmers' donated iron tools.

James Watt did not invent the steam engine; Thomas Newcomen had built working ones decades earlier for pumping water out of mines. Watt's 1769 patent added a separate condenser, so the cylinder no longer had to be cooled and reheated on every stroke, cutting fuel use dramatically and making steam power practical well beyond mine sites for the first time.

Watt reached the idea while repairing a model Newcomen engine at Glasgow University and spent years afterward refining it with the manufacturer Matthew Boulton, who financed the venture. Their engines went on to drive cotton mills, ironworks and eventually locomotives, giving factories a power source that no longer depended on a river or a windy hillside.

Before Djoser's tomb at Saqqara, Egyptian royal burials were low rectangular mounds of mud brick called mastabas. His architect, Imhotep, stacked six mastabas of decreasing size on top of each other in cut limestone, producing a stepped tower roughly sixty metres tall around 2650 BCE, the first building of its scale made almost entirely of stone.

Imhotep is one of the few named architects to survive from ancient Egypt at all; later inscriptions credit him and, centuries afterward, Egyptians worshipped him as a god of medicine and wisdom. The step pyramid's surrounding complex, walled courtyards and dummy buildings, still stands beneath the sand at Saqqara today.

By around 2500 BCE the sarsen stones at Stonehenge, some weighing over twenty tonnes, had been dragged roughly thirty kilometres from the Marlborough Downs and raised into the trilithon arrangement still visible today. The smaller bluestones inside the ring came from much further, a set of Welsh hills over 200 kilometres away, a haulage distance that still has no settled explanation.

The stones were shaped with mortice and tenon joints borrowed from woodworking, locking lintels onto their uprights rather than simply balancing them. Excavated cremated remains, dating across several centuries around this period, show the site kept being used as a burial ground even as its stone architecture was still being finished.

The first phase at Stonehenge was not a ring of tall stones but a circular ditch and bank enclosing a ring of pits, later known as the Aubrey Holes, dug into Salisbury Plain around 3000 BCE. Some pits held cremated human remains, making the site a cemetery centuries before the sarsens most visitors recognise were ever moved into place.

The famous upright stones came much later, raised in stages from around 2500 BCE. That gap of roughly five hundred years between the ditch and the stone circle is easy to miss when the monument is treated as a single construction rather than a project reworked by generations who never met its first builders.

The canal opened on 17 November 1869 after ten years of digging by a workforce that at times relied on forced Egyptian labour, a practice the project's financier, Ferdinand de Lesseps, only phased out after European objections and the introduction of steam dredgers. It let ships sail between Europe and Asia without rounding Africa, cutting thousands of miles from the route.

Egypt's ruler had bought a large stake in the venture to help finance it, but mounting debt forced the sale of Egypt's shares to Britain in 1875. That purchase gave Britain a controlling interest in the waterway and helped draw the country into occupying Egypt seven years later.

On 9 May 1980 the freighter Summit Venture, blinded by a squall, struck a support column of the old Sunshine Skyway and dropped a 396 metre section of roadway into Tampa Bay, killing thirty-five people, most of them in a bus and cars that drove straight off the broken edge. The replacement opened in 1987 as a cable-stayed span built to survive exactly that kind of impact.

Its single tower and yellow cables were designed with reinforced dolphin piers, artificial islands meant to stop a ship before it ever reaches the bridge deck. The new Skyway also carries a fixed span roughly 15 metres higher than its predecessor, giving large vessels far more clearance as they pass beneath.

Norman Foster's tower at 30 St Mary Axe has a diagrid steel frame wrapped in a spiralling pattern of glass, a curved profile chosen to reduce wind loading on the ground and let air circulate up through gaps in the floor plates instead of relying purely on mechanical ventilation. Londoners nicknamed it the Gherkin almost as soon as construction topped out, and the name displaced the developer's own branding within its first year.

It opened in 2003 on the site of the Baltic Exchange, which had been badly damaged by an IRA bomb in 1992, and became the City of London's first tall building designed explicitly around energy efficiency rather than maximum floor area. It was sold in 2007 for a sum that, at the time, made it Britain's most expensive office building.

A man on a horse rode across the deck before the ribbon was cut. Francis de Groot, a member of a right wing paramilitary group opposed to the state premier, slashed the ceremonial ribbon with his sword ahead of the official opening on 19 March 1932, delaying the real ceremony by minutes and making the front pages instead of the bridge itself.

The single steel arch, built to carry trains, trams and cars between the city and the north shore, was for decades the widest long span bridge in the world by deck width. It held that particular distinction until wider road decks elsewhere overtook it. Sixteen men died during its eight years of construction, mostly from falls.

Danish architect Jorn Utzon won the 1957 design competition with sketches so rough that some judges initially rejected them before senior judge Eero Saarinen insisted on a second look. Work on the podium began in 1959 before Utzon had actually solved how to build the shell shaped roofs he had drawn, a gap that stalled the site for years.

The solution, arrived at only after 1961, was to base every shell on sections of a single sphere so the curved concrete ribs could be precast rather than individually moulded. Cost overruns and political pressure eventually drove Utzon to resign in 1966, years before the building opened, and he never returned to see it finished.

Danish architect Jorn Utzon won the 1957 design competition with sketches of sail-like shells, but nobody, including Utzon, yet knew how to build them. Engineers spent years searching for a workable geometry before realising that every shell could be carved from sections of the same imaginary sphere, letting them be cast from standardised moulds rather than shaped individually.

Utzon resigned in 1966 amid disputes over cost and design control with the New South Wales government and never saw the building finished or, for decades, set foot in it again. The project's budget grew from an original estimate of about 7 million Australian dollars to roughly 102 million by the time it opened in October 1973, largely funded through a dedicated lottery rather than general taxation.

Taipei sits in an earthquake zone prone to typhoons, so the tower's engineers hung a 660-tonne steel pendulum, visible through windows near the top, to counteract sway from wind and tremors. The building's 101 storeys are grouped visually into eight repeating sections of eight floors each, a number chosen for its associations with prosperity in Chinese culture rather than for structural reasons.

It opened on 31 December 2004 at 508 metres and was immediately the tallest building in the world, a title it held for just over five years. The Burj Khalifa overtook it in January 2010, though Taipei 101's damper and record-setting elevators, which travelled at up to 60 kilometres per hour, kept it a reference point for supertall design well after it lost the height record.

Shah Jahan began the Taj Mahal in 1632 after the death of his wife Mumtaz Mahal during childbirth, ordering a tomb built in white marble brought from Rajasthan along with inlaid gemstones sourced from as far as Afghanistan and Sri Lanka. Roughly 20,000 workers laboured on the site over the following two decades.

A popular story claims Shah Jahan had his workers' hands cut off afterward so the design could never be repeated, a tale with no contemporary evidence behind it. He was later deposed by his own son and spent his final years imprisoned in Agra Fort, from where he could see the tomb across the river.

Shah Jahan built the mausoleum for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. The main structure was largely finished by 1643, but the surrounding gardens, gateway and outbuildings kept craftsmen working for another decade, and 1653 is usually given as the year the whole complex was finally done.

Twenty thousand workers and craftsmen were brought in from across the Mughal empire and beyond, and the white marble was hauled from a quarry in Rajasthan, some 250 miles away, on a fleet of specially built carts and elephants. Shah Jahan was later buried beside Mumtaz Mahal in the same tomb he had spent decades having built for her.

The Tang court garrisoned outposts across the Tarim Basin and beyond to keep the Silk Road's oasis towns, places like Kucha and Khotan, open and taxable, turning a loose caravan route into something closer to a managed corridor backed by imperial soldiers and administrators.

That reach broke in 751 at the Battle of Talas, where Tang forces lost to an Abbasid army near the Talas River, and Tang influence in Central Asia contracted afterward. Chinese papermakers are said to have been among the prisoners taken, one route by which papermaking reached the Islamic world.

The Brihadeeswarar Temple's vimana, its tower over the main shrine, rises about 66 metres in thirteen tapering tiers, capped by a single dome-shaped stone weighing roughly eighty tonnes. How Chola builders lifted that block into place without cranes is still debated; one long-standing account describes a ramp built from a village several kilometres away to raise it gradually.

Rajaraja I completed the temple around 1010 to mark his conquests and to house a colossal stone lingam carved from a single piece of granite. For a time its tower was the tallest of its kind in India, a record eventually surpassed by later temple towers built under his successors and other South Indian dynasties.

Bankside Power Station stopped generating electricity in 1981 and sat empty on the Thames for over a decade before the Tate chose it over more than seventy other sites for a new gallery of international modern art. The architects Herzog and de Meuron kept the brick shell and the single central chimney almost untouched, gutting the turbine hall into a vast entrance space rather than disguising the building's industrial origin.

It opened in May 2000 and drew about 5.25 million visitors in its first year, far more than its planners had forecast, which forced an extension built over the following decade to add gallery space the original conversion had not budgeted for. The turbine hall itself became known for a running series of oversized temporary installations rather than paintings.

Samuel Morse was not the first to build an electric telegraph; British inventors William Cooke and Charles Wheatstone had patented a working system in 1837 as well, and earlier experimental telegraphs existed before either. Morse's contribution, developed with Alfred Vail from 1837, paired a simple single wire system with a code of dots and dashes that was cheap to build and easy to learn.

Morse demonstrated his device to Congress and got funding in 1843 for a line between Washington and Baltimore, sending the message What hath God wrought when it opened the following year. The code and the low cost of his equipment let it spread across America and much of the world faster than the more elaborate British system.

Philo Farnsworth transmitted the first electronic television image, a simple line, from his San Francisco laboratory in September 1927, having sketched the idea for an image dissector tube as a teenager. He was still in his early twenties and largely self-taught, financing the work through investors who grew impatient waiting for a marketable product.

Farnsworth's claim to the invention was contested for years by RCA, whose researcher Vladimir Zworykin had filed an earlier patent application for a similar tube that did not yet work. A patent court eventually sided with Farnsworth in 1934, but RCA's marketing power meant it, not Farnsworth, dominated television's commercial rollout in the following decade.

Seven columns are what remain, not the whole building. The Temple of Apollo at Corinth, raised around 540 BCE, replaced a 7th century predecessor destroyed by fire, and originally carried six columns at each short end and fifteen along each side, all cut as monolithic drums rather than stacked sections.

Those surviving seven are the oldest Doric columns still standing intact anywhere in mainland Greece, which is why the temple is treated as a benchmark for the order's early form: thick, squat shafts with almost no taper, built before Doric proportions settled into the leaner style seen later at Athens.

Construction on the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan began around 100 CE, using an estimated three million tonnes of rubble and adobe piled into a base wider than the Great Pyramid of Giza, though considerably lower at about 65 metres. The city that grew around it eventually held well over a hundred thousand people, making it one of the largest urban centres anywhere in the world at the time.

Beneath the pyramid, archaeologists found a natural cave system that may have been treated as sacred ground before construction started, suggesting the site was chosen rather than arbitrary. Teotihuacan's own name for the pyramid is unknown; Sun and Moon were labels the later Aztecs gave the abandoned ruins centuries after the city itself had collapsed.

Qin Shi Huang unified China's warring states in 221 BCE and then spent decades preparing a tomb complex near Xi'an that no one was meant to see. Around it, buried in pits, an army of over 8,000 life-size clay soldiers stood in battle formation, each face individually modelled, facing east toward the states he had conquered.

Farmers digging a well found the first fragments in 1974, more than two thousand years after burial. Excavation is still incomplete: the emperor's central tomb mound has never been opened, partly out of caution about preserving whatever lies inside once the seal is broken.

Filling the reservoir behind the Three Gorges Dam meant flooding thirteen cities, over a hundred towns and roughly 1,300 archaeological sites along the Yangtze, displacing more than a million people in a resettlement programme that ran across more than a decade of construction. The dam wall itself, over 2 kilometres wide and 181 metres tall, was completed in stages between 2003 and 2006 as the reservoir rose behind it.

By installed capacity it is the largest hydroelectric power station ever built, generating far more electricity than the Itaipu Dam on the Brazil-Paraguay border, its nearest rival by output. Its ship lift and locks were built partly to preserve river trade through the gorges that its own reservoir had submerged under water up to 175 metres deep.

Tikal's Great Plaza was rebuilt in stages for centuries before reaching the form visible today around 700, under rulers including Jasaw Chan Kawiil I, whose Temple I pyramid rises about 47 metres over the plaza's eastern side, facing the slightly shorter Temple II across the open space.
