The city these temples anchored held an estimated population in the tens of thousands at its height, supported by reservoirs cut into the limestone bedrock to store rainwater through the dry season, since Tikal sits far from any permanent river or lake in the Guatemalan lowlands.

Tiwanaku sits at over 3,800 metres above sea level near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, a height at which farming and large-scale building are both unusually hard. Its builders raised platform mounds and gateways from precisely cut stone blocks, some weighing many tonnes, fitted so closely that little or no mortar was needed.

The site's raised-field agriculture around the lake supported a population large enough to sustain long-distance building projects, and its influence spread through the southern Andes via trade and religious pilgrimage rather than conquest. Tiwanaku declined sharply after around 1000, likely tied to a prolonged drought that undermined the farming its monuments depended on.

Tula, the Toltec capital north of modern Mexico City, rose centuries after Teotihuacan's collapse but borrowed its architectural language, building stepped pyramids topped with colonnaded halls and, distinctively, rows of basalt warrior columns carved in relief, rather than plain stone piers.

Those warrior columns and feathered-serpent motifs turn up again at Chichen Itza hundreds of kilometres away, a resemblance close enough that historians still argue over whether Toltecs migrated there, traded ideas with it, or whether both cities simply drew on a shared older Mesoamerican tradition.

Tower Bridge opened on 30 June 1894 after eight years of construction, built to ease traffic across the Thames without blocking tall ships heading for the busy docks upstream of London Bridge. Its solution was a bascule design: two roadway sections that hinge upward on hydraulic machinery, originally powered by steam engines that were only replaced with electric pumps in 1976.

The stone Gothic towers are largely decorative, clad around a steel frame chosen so the bridge would match the nearby Tower of London rather than look like the industrial ironwork it actually is. In 1952 a bus driver had to accelerate across a gap as the bascules began to rise beneath him after a signalling error, an incident the bridge's operators still cite in staff training.

William the Conqueror began the White Tower around 1078 to overawe a recently conquered London, using imported Caen stone from Normandy rather than local materials, a deliberate display that the new rulers could command resources across the Channel. The fortress grew over subsequent reigns into the concentric castle of walls and towers that stands today.

Its uses ranged far beyond defence: it held the royal mint, an armoury, a menagerie that once included lions and a polar bear, and a prison whose inmates included Anne Boleyn and, centuries later, Rudolf Hess. The Crown Jewels have been kept there since the seventeenth century.

A continuous carved frieze spirals up the column for roughly 190 metres, wrapping it 23 times to tell the story of Trajan's wars against Dacia in modern Romania. Originally the scenes were painted in colour, and a bronze statue of the emperor stood on top until it was lost in the Middle Ages and replaced with a statue of Saint Peter in 1588.

The column doubled as a tomb: a chamber at its base once held a golden urn with Trajan's ashes. Later emperors used it as a model rather than a rival, and Rome's other great carved column, the Column of Marcus Aurelius, borrowed the same spiral format decades afterward.

Aramco built the pipeline, known as Tapline, to avoid shipping Saudi crude the long way around Arabia by tanker through the Persian Gulf and Suez. It ran roughly 1,650 kilometres from the oilfields near Abqaiq across Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Syria to the Lebanese port of Sidon on the Mediterranean, cutting the journey to European markets by weeks.

Tapline created towns and jobs along a route that had previously been mostly desert track, and it operated for over four decades. Repeated closures from regional conflict and disputes over transit fees eroded its usefulness, and the line was finally shut down for good in 1990.

The main line between Moscow and Vladivostok opened in July 1904 after thirteen years of construction ordered by Tsar Alexander III, running roughly 9,300 kilometres and remaining the longest single railway line in the world today. Convict and exile labour built long stretches of it through Siberian forest and permafrost, in conditions that killed workers from cold, disease and rockfalls.

Work continued for over a decade after the 1904 opening, including a shorter route around Lake Baikal that replaced an earlier ferry crossing and a bridge over the Amur River finished only in 1916. The railway allowed Russia to move troops and settlers east far faster than before, reshaping Siberia's economy within a generation.

Architect William Pereira gave the Transamerica Pyramid its tapered shape in 1972 partly to let more daylight and open sky reach the streets below, rather than casting the dense shadow a boxy tower of the same height would. At 260 metres it became San Francisco's tallest building on completion, a title it held for decades before being overtaken by the Salesforce Tower in 2018.

Two narrow wings jut from the sides near the top, housing an elevator shaft and a smoking lounge, the only parts of the tower that break its otherwise unbroken pyramid outline. Locals and the press mocked the design as a joke before it opened, but the building became one of the city's most photographed landmarks, appearing in its official seal alongside the Golden Gate Bridge.

The ship Great Eastern left Valentia Island, Ireland, in July 1866 carrying over 2,700 nautical miles of cable, and reached Heart's Content, Newfoundland, fourteen days later with a working line. It was not the first attempt: an 1858 cable had briefly connected the continents before failing within weeks, and an 1865 attempt had snapped and been lost at sea.

The 1866 cable carried messages at roughly eight words a minute, slow by later standards but eighty times faster than its 1858 predecessor. The Great Eastern then went back, recovered the lost 1865 cable from the seabed, spliced it, and completed it too, so that by September two working lines crossed the Atlantic instead of none.

On 10 May 1869 the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, where a ceremonial golden spike was driven into a polished laurel tie. The Central Pacific's track east from California relied heavily on Chinese immigrant labourers, who cut through the Sierra Nevada by hand and black powder, often in winter conditions that killed dozens.

The link cut the journey between the coasts from months by wagon to about a week by train, and it reshaped where towns and industries grew along its route. Promontory Summit itself, chosen partly for convenience, was later bypassed by a shorter route across the Great Salt Lake and today survives mainly as a historic site.

Eupalinos built his tunnel around 530 BCE to bring water from a spring on the far side of a mountain into the fortified city of Samos, keeping the pipeline hidden from any besieging enemy who might otherwise cut it off. The finished passage ran 1,036 metres straight through solid rock.

Two crews dug from opposite ends at once, using geometry to keep both headings aimed correctly with no way to check progress against the surface above. When they met in the middle, the two tunnels were offset by only about 60 centimetres in height, an accuracy that would be difficult even with today's basic instruments, let alone the sightlines and rods Eupalinos had.

Eero Saarinen never called his TWA terminal a bird, though the comparison stuck the moment it opened at Idlewild Airport, later renamed JFK, in 1962. The four vaulted concrete shells rise and curve toward the sky, and inside there is barely a straight line: the ticket counters, staircases and even the departure boards were custom-shaped to match the building's flow rather than fitted into it afterward.

Saarinen died of a brain tumour in 1961, a year before the terminal opened, and never saw it in use. Jet-age airliners soon outgrew the gates he had designed for propeller planes and early jets, and the building stopped handling flights in 2001. It reopened in 2019 as a hotel, its shells preserved as the lobby rather than demolished for a larger terminal.

John D. Rockefeller Jr. bought the East River site, a former slaughterhouse and rail yard district, and donated it to the United Nations after the organisation's search for a home elsewhere had stalled. An international team of architects worked under Wallace Harrison, including Le Corbusier and Oscar Niemeyer, though their competing visions for the site produced friction Harrison had to resolve himself.

The Secretariat tower, a slab of glass and marble finished in 1950, became a template copied by office buildings worldwide long before the wider complex was finished in 1952. The land the UN sits on is technically international territory, not part of New York City, though it remains subject to most local laws by agreement.

The staircase now most associated with the Vatican Museums was designed by engineer Giuseppe Momo in 1932, not by Donato Bramante, whose separate and much older square spiral staircase from around 1505 sits elsewhere in the palace and is often confused with it. Momo's version consists of two ramps wound around a single shaft in a double helix, so people can climb and descend without ever meeting on the stairs.

Its ironwork balustrade and terracotta-coloured steps were built to serve as the museums' grand exit, letting large crowds leave in one continuous flow rather than queuing on a single staircase. Photographers now treat it as one of the most recognisable images inside the Vatican, framed from directly above to show the two spirals nesting around each other.

NASA finished the Vehicle Assembly Building at Kennedy Space Center in 1966 to stack Saturn V rockets vertically before rolling them to the launch pad on a crawler. At 160 metres it was built tall enough to enclose a fully assembled Saturn V, engine to nose cone, with room above for the overhead cranes that lifted each stage into place.

The building is so large that its interior air handling has to fight condensation forming under its own roof on humid Florida days, effectively generating indoor weather. Giant American flag and NASA logo panels painted on its exterior are each roughly the size of a basketball court, a scale chosen so the markings would still register from miles away across the flat Florida scrubland.

When the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge opened on 21 November 1964, its main span of 1,298 metres beat the Golden Gate Bridge by about 18 metres, making it briefly the longest suspension span on earth. Robert Moses pushed the project through against opposition from residents of Bay Ridge and Staten Island, whose neighbourhoods lost hundreds of homes to the approaches.

The bridge's twin towers are almost four centimetres further apart at the top than at the base, a gap engineers had to build in deliberately because the earth's curvature pulls two tall, parallel verticals slightly out of true. It held the world record for 17 years, until England's Humber Bridge overtook it in 1981, and it is still the longest suspension bridge in the Americas.

Versailles began as Louis XIII's modest hunting lodge, a place his son had no fondness for at first. Louis XIV rebuilt it into a seat of government almost out of spite for Paris, where he had lived through the frightening street uprisings of the Fronde as a child, and by 1682 he moved his entire court and administration there permanently.

The move put roughly three thousand nobles, courtiers and officials under one roof, alongside thousands more servants, and turned attendance at Versailles into a political necessity: a nobleman who stayed away lost influence at court. Louis used the palace's rigid daily ceremonies, dressing and dining in public, to keep the aristocracy watched and occupied rather than plotting in their own provinces.

Nero had drained an artificial lake south of the Palatine to build the grounds of his Golden House, a private estate carved out of land burned in the great fire of 64. Vespasian chose that exact spot in 72 to start his amphitheatre, replacing an emperor's pleasure gardens with a building meant for the whole city.

Money for the project came from the spoils of the Jewish War, which Vespasian and his son Titus had just finished putting down in Judaea. Vespasian did not live to see it open; he died in 79, a year before Titus dedicated the finished amphitheatre with games that reportedly ran for a hundred days.

Irish architect James Hoban won a design competition for the presidential residence, and construction ran from 1792 to 1800 using enslaved and free labourers alongside European stonemasons. John Adams became the first president to live there in November 1800, moving into a building whose plaster was still drying and whose grounds were still a construction site.

The sandstone exterior was originally whitewashed with a lime mixture to protect it from moisture, which is where its familiar colour came from long before it carried the name officially. British troops burned the interior during the War of 1812, and Hoban was brought back to rebuild it, reopening it for James Monroe in 1817.

The Winter Palace on the Neva was the fourth palace built on or near the site for the Romanovs, designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli for Empress Elizabeth and finished in 1762, the year she died without seeing it in use. It housed roughly 1,500 rooms and became the official winter residence of the Russian tsars for the century and a half that followed.

It was here that a crowd of unarmed petitioners was fired on by troops in 1905, an event remembered as Bloody Sunday, and it was the Provisional Government's seat when Bolshevik forces stormed it in October 1917. The palace now forms the core of the State Hermitage Museum, one of the largest art collections in the world.

Construction on the World Trade Center's twin towers began in August 1968 on landfill created from the excavated site itself, soil and rock dug out for the foundations dumped into the Hudson River to extend Manhattan's shoreline by several blocks. The towers used a then-unusual tube structure, with steel columns packed close along the exterior walls taking the load rather than a dense internal skeleton.

Minoru Yamasaki designed narrow windows just 45 centimetres wide, partly for structural reasons and partly because he was uneasy with heights himself and wanted occupants to feel enclosed rather than exposed. The North Tower topped out in 1970 and the South Tower in 1971, and together they briefly held the title of the world's tallest building before Chicago's Sears Tower overtook them in 1973.

King Ur-Nammu began the Great Ziggurat of Ur around 2100 BCE as a stepped mud-brick platform for a shrine to the moon god Nanna, set at the top rather than inside the structure itself. The core was built of sun-dried mud brick, faced with fired brick set in bitumen to shed rain, a construction detail that let much of it survive.

The building fell into ruin over the following centuries until Nabonidus, Babylon's last king, restored it in the sixth century BCE. British archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated and partially reconstructed the lower stages in the 1920s, and its restored silhouette is largely his interpretation rather than the untouched original.
